name: Metal Roofing
title: Metal Roofing Northern Colorado
description: Metal roofing in Northern Colorado: standing seam, metal shingles, stone-coated steel, and screw-down panels built for hail and snow. Get a free quote.
lede: Metal is not one product. It is five different roof systems that share a material and little else. We install all of them, and the first job is telling you which one your roof, your budget, and your insurer actually call for.
summary: Standing seam, metal shingle, stone-coated steel, and exposed-fastener metal roofing for Colorado homes, HOAs, and commercial buildings.
costRange: $650 to $1,800 per square installed, by system

sections.h2: What metal roofing is, and the five systems under that name
sections.html:
When a homeowner says they want a metal roof, they usually mean a picture in their head. The picture is almost always standing seam. But the metal roofing category covers five distinct systems, and they do not perform the same, cost the same, or belong on the same buildings.

  • Standing seam. Vertical panels, 12 to 18 inches wide, joined at raised seams with concealed clips and no exposed screws in the field of the roof. The longest-lived and most weather-tight option. It has its own page: standing seam metal roofing.
  • Exposed-fastener panels. R-panel, PBR, and corrugated profiles screwed straight through the panel into purlins or decking, with a rubber washer under every screw head. The lowest cost metal roof. Common on shops, barns, agricultural buildings, and budget commercial work.
  • Metal shingles and shakes. Stamped steel or aluminum panels, usually four-way interlocking, formed to look like shake, slate, or tile. Lightweight and HOA-friendly in neighborhoods that will not approve vertical panels.
  • Stone-coated steel. Steel panels with an acrylic-bonded stone granule surface. Hides hail impacts well and reads as a shingle or tile roof from the street.
  • Corrugated and ribbed sheet. The classic wavy profile, now sold in heavier gauges and painted finishes for modern and rustic designs.

Under all five, the parts that decide whether the roof lasts are the same: the gauge of the steel, the paint system, the underlayment, and the flashing and penetration details.

sections.h2: Why metal suits Colorado
sections.html:
Colorado is a hard place for a roof, and metal answers most of what makes it hard.

Hail on the Front Range. The corridor from Fort Collins through Loveland, Longmont, and Denver sees some of the most frequent damaging hail in the country, and the May 2017 storm remains the state's costliest insured hail event at more than two billion dollars. Many steel panel, metal shingle, and stone-coated steel products carry a UL 2218 Class 4 rating, meaning a 2 inch steel ball dropped from 20 feet does not crack or split the panel. Class 4 is the rating most Colorado carriers discount.

UV at altitude. At 5,000 feet and above, ultraviolet exposure is stronger than at sea level, and it chalks and fades cheap paint fast. A PVDF finish, sold under the Kynar 500 name, holds color far longer than siliconized polyester (SMP), and we treat it as the baseline on any roof you expect to keep for decades.

Snow load and ice dams. Larimer County design ground snow loads run from 55 pounds per square foot around 5,000 feet to 110 pounds per square foot at 8,000 feet. Metal sheds snow, which is a benefit over entries and a hazard over walkways, so snow retention is designed into every mountain installation.

Wildfire. Steel is non-combustible and installs as a Class A assembly, which is what Colorado's Wildfire Resiliency Code requires in mapped wildland urban interface zones, now enforced in towns like Estes Park and Nederland.

Wind. Concealed-clip systems are tested for uplift, and downslope wind events along the foothills are where screw-down roofs with aged washers start to lift.

sections.h2: Lifespan and maintenance by system
sections.html:
Lifespan on a metal roof is set by three things: the gauge, the paint, and the fasteners.

SystemTypical service lifeWhat ages it
Standing seam, 24 gauge, PVDF40 to 70 yearsFlashing sealants, very large hail
Metal shingle and stone-coated steel40 to 60 yearsGranule loss, fastener corrosion at cut edges
Exposed fastener, 26 or 29 gauge20 to 35 yearsScrew washers dry out and back out, panel oil-canning, rust at laps

Maintenance is light but not zero. Every few years someone should walk the roof and check sealant at pipe boots, skylight curbs, and wall flashings, clear debris from valleys and behind chimneys, and confirm snow guards are tight. On an exposed-fastener roof, plan on re-driving or replacing screws at 10 to 15 years, because a loose screw is a leak path. We include a fastener count and sealant check in every free roof inspection on a metal roof.

Two honest notes. Large hail can dent smooth panels without causing a leak, and some policies exclude that cosmetic damage, so ask your agent how your policy reads before you buy. And oil canning, the slight waviness you can see in flat panels at a low sun angle, is a property of sheet metal, not a defect. Striations, a heavier gauge, and narrower panels reduce it.

sections.h2: What metal roofing costs in Colorado
sections.html:
Metal is sold by the square, which is 100 square feet of roof. Typical installed ranges in Northern Colorado right now, including tear-off of one shingle layer and synthetic underlayment:

  • Exposed-fastener panels: roughly $650 to $1,100 per square
  • Stone-coated steel and metal shingles: roughly $900 to $1,500 per square
  • Standing seam, 24 gauge, PVDF: roughly $1,100 to $1,800 per square

Those are planning numbers, not quotes. The real figure varies by pitch, access, tear-off, decking condition, and detailing: a cut-up roof with six valleys, three chimneys, and a dozen penetrations costs much more per square than a simple gable. Mountain homes add snow retention, high-temperature ice and water shield across the entire deck, and longer travel. Expect metal to run two to three times the installed cost of architectural asphalt shingles, and then weigh that against the roof lasting through two or three asphalt replacement cycles. We lay that math out in our 30 year metal versus asphalt comparison, and financing is available on qualifying projects.

sections.h2: Warranty: what to ask for in writing
sections.html:
A metal roof comes with two or three separate warranties, and they cover different things.

Paint finish warranty. Issued by the coil coater, typically 30 to 40 years on PVDF against chalk and fade beyond a stated measurement, usually shorter on SMP. It covers the paint, not leaks.

Substrate warranty. Covers the steel itself against perforation from rust, often 20 to 25 years on Galvalume, with exclusions near salt or for cut edges left unsealed.

Weathertightness warranty. On commercial standing seam, a manufacturer can inspect the installation and issue a system warranty that actually covers leaks. These are rarer on residential jobs and require the installer to be approved by the manufacturer.

Workmanship warranty. This is the one that matters most in the first years, because nearly every early leak traces to flashing, penetrations, or fastening, not the panel. Ask that it be written, state the term in years, cover labor and materials to repair the leak and interior damage caused by the workmanship defect, and name who answers the phone if the company changes hands.

Before you sign, ask for the panel manufacturer and model, the gauge, the paint system by name, the underlayment type, the clip or fastener type, and a drawing of snow retention placement. If an estimate does not list those, you cannot compare it to one that does.

faq.q: How long does a metal roof last in Colorado?
faq.a: A standing seam roof in 24 gauge steel with a PVDF finish is commonly expected to last 40 to 70 years in Colorado. Metal shingles and stone-coated steel run 40 to 60. Exposed-fastener panels last 20 to 35 years, because the rubber washers under the screws dry out and need attention long before the steel does. High-altitude UV is the main reason to insist on a PVDF paint system rather than a cheaper polyester finish.

faq.q: Does hail dent a metal roof?
faq.a: Large hail can leave cosmetic dents on smooth, flat panels, though dents rarely cause leaks. Textured and striated panels, metal shingles, and stone-coated steel hide impacts far better, and many of those products carry UL 2218 Class 4 ratings. The real issue is your policy: some Colorado carriers add a cosmetic damage exclusion on metal roofs. Ask your agent how your policy handles dents before you choose a panel.

faq.q: Will my insurance give a discount for a metal roof?
faq.a: Many Colorado insurers discount premiums for roof coverings with a UL 2218 Class 4 impact rating, and a lot of metal products qualify. The discount amount and the paperwork vary by carrier. We provide the product listing and installation documentation so you can submit it to your agent, and we tell you up front if the specific panel you are considering is not Class 4 listed.

faq.q: Can you install a metal roof over my existing shingles?
faq.a: It is sometimes allowed by code over a single layer, but we usually recommend a tear-off. Removing the shingles lets us inspect and repair the decking, install high-temperature ice and water shield where it is needed, fasten clips into sound wood, and keep the manufacturer warranty clean. Going over old shingles saves a few hundred dollars per square and can cost much more later if the deck underneath is soft.

faq.q: Is a metal roof loud when it rains?
faq.a: Not when it is installed over solid decking with underlayment, which is how every residential metal roof we install goes down. The loud tin roof people remember is a bare panel over open framing on a barn or shed. On a house with a deck, underlayment, attic insulation, and drywall between you and the roof, rain on metal is about as loud as rain on asphalt shingles.

name: Standing Seam Metal Roofing
h1: Standing Seam Metal Roofing in Colorado
title: Standing Seam Metal Roof Colorado
description: Standing seam metal roofing in Colorado: snap-lock and mechanically seamed panels, 24 gauge steel, PVDF finish, snow retention. Get a free inspection.
lede: Standing seam is the metal roof that mountain architects draw and Front Range homeowners choose when they are done re-roofing after every hail season. The details that make it last are invisible from the driveway, so here they are.
summary: Concealed-fastener standing seam roofing, snap-lock and mechanically seamed, with engineered clips and snow retention for Colorado homes and commercial buildings.

sections.h2: What standing seam is, panel by panel
sections.html:
A standing seam roof is a series of vertical metal panels, usually 12 to 18 inches wide and run in one continuous length from eave to ridge, joined at raised seams that stand 1 to 2 inches above the flat of the panel. Clips hidden inside each seam hold the panel to the deck. No screw penetrates the weather surface anywhere in the field of the roof. That single fact is why standing seam outlasts every other metal roofing system.

The two families you will be quoted:

  • Snap-lock. The male and female legs of adjacent panels snap together over a clip by hand. No seaming machine, faster installation, lower labor cost. Suitable on slopes of 3:12 and steeper.
  • Mechanically seamed. The panel legs are crimped together with a powered seamer, either a single 90 degree fold or a double 180 degree fold. Double-lock seams are the most weather-tight assembly in roofing and can go down to slopes as low as 1:12 with sealant in the seam. This is the system for low-slope commercial retrofits, mountain homes, and anywhere wind-driven snow will sit on the roof.

Panel profiles vary by seam height, width, and whether the flat is smooth, striated, or has pencil ribs. Striations stiffen the panel and reduce oil canning, which is why we rarely recommend a wide smooth-flat panel on a residential roof facing the street.

Gauge matters. We specify 24 gauge steel as the residential standard. 26 gauge is thinner, oil-cans more, dents easier, and the savings are small. 22 gauge shows up on commercial work and high-exposure mountain roofs.

sections.h2: Why standing seam suits Colorado
sections.html:
Thermal movement. A 40 foot steel panel on a south-facing Colorado roof can swing 150 degrees between a January night and a July afternoon, and it grows and shrinks roughly half an inch over that range. Screw-down roofs fight that movement and elongate their fastener holes. Standing seam uses floating clips, a two-piece clip with a sliding tab, that let the panel move while the clip stays fixed to the deck. On panels longer than about 30 feet, floating clips are not optional; they are the difference between a 50 year roof and a roof with torn seams at year 12.

Hail. Steel panels in 24 gauge from most major coil sources are tested to UL 2218 Class 4. The seam geometry spreads impact, and striated panels hide the shallow dents that very large hail can leave.

Snow and ice in the mountains. A mechanically seamed roof over a continuous high-temperature ice and water membrane is the assembly we trust at 8,000 feet in Breckenridge, Winter Park, and Grand Lake. Snow slides off smooth metal, which prevents ice dams but creates an avalanche hazard, so snow retention is engineered to the pitch, panel length, and ground snow load: clamp-on bar or fence systems that grip the seam without a single hole, placed in rows above entries, decks, gas meters, and anything below the eave you do not want buried. Our mountain roofing guide goes deeper.

Wildfire and wind. Steel is non-combustible and meets the Class A requirement of Colorado's Wildfire Resiliency Code. Clip-held seams resist uplift better than any exposed-fastener panel, which matters on foothill lots in the path of downslope wind.

UV. A PVDF finish, sold as Kynar 500 and similar names, uses a resin that is at least 70 percent fluoropolymer. It is the only paint we specify above 5,000 feet.

sections.h2: Lifespan and maintenance
sections.html:
Plan on 50 to 70 years from a 24 gauge, PVDF-coated, mechanically seamed roof with floating clips on a properly detailed deck. The steel will not be what fails. What ages on a standing seam roof is the accessory list: sealant at pipe boots and curb flashings (15 to 20 years), gaskets on snow guard clamps, and the butyl tape in seams on low-slope installations. A walk-through every three to five years, with a sealant touch-up and a check that snow retention hardware is torqued, keeps the system whole.

Things that shorten the life of a standing seam roof, all of them installer decisions:

  • Fixed clips on long panels, which tears the seam or buckles the panel as it moves
  • Face-screwing trim and ridge caps instead of using concealed cleats
  • Running panels over old shingles with no slip sheet, which prints every granule through the finish
  • Standard ice and water shield instead of high-temperature membrane under a dark roof, which melts and bleeds asphalt
  • Snow guards glued or face-screwed instead of clamped to the seam

If you are weighing standing seam against Class 4 asphalt or a synthetic slate or shake roof, the relevant comparison is total cost over 30 years, not the first invoice.

sections.h2: What standing seam costs in Colorado, and the premium over screw-down
sections.html:
Typical installed ranges in Northern Colorado for 24 gauge steel with a PVDF finish, including tear-off of one layer, synthetic underlayment, and standard flashings:

  • Snap-lock standing seam: roughly $1,100 to $1,500 per square
  • Mechanically seamed, single lock: roughly $1,300 to $1,700 per square
  • Mechanically seamed, double lock, low slope or mountain spec: roughly $1,500 to $1,800 per square or more

Expect 40 to 70 percent more than an exposed-fastener panel roof on the same house. The premium buys concealed clips, seamed joints, and a roof that does not need its fasteners serviced every decade. Full-deck high-temperature ice and water shield, engineered snow retention, and copper or stainless accessories add to the mountain-home number.

Every figure above varies by pitch, access, tear-off, decking, and detailing. Narrow panels cost more per square than wide ones. A simple gable with two long runs can come in below range; a roof with dormers, hips, and a dozen penetrations will come in above it, because each one is a hand-formed flashing. Request an itemized estimate so you can see those line items, and read how to read a roofing estimate before you compare bids.

sections.h2: Warranty: the three documents to ask for
sections.html:
Finish warranty. The coil coater warrants the PVDF paint, commonly 35 to 40 years against chalking and fading past a measured threshold, with a shorter film-integrity term. Ask for the actual certificate with the color and coil lot on it, not a brochure.

Substrate warranty. Covers rust-through of the base steel, often 20 to 25 years. It usually excludes cut edges that were never sealed, which is why we hem exposed edges at eaves and seal them.

Weathertightness warranty. Available on commercial projects when the manufacturer inspects the installation and the installer is on their approved list. It covers leaks, not just materials, and it is worth asking whether your project qualifies.

Workmanship warranty. A standing seam roof that leaks in year three leaks at a flashing, a curb, a transition, or a ridge, and none of that is covered by the manufacturer. Get the workmanship term in writing, confirm it covers labor and materials, and confirm it transfers if you sell. A free inspection is the first step on any standing seam project.

faq.q: What is the difference between snap-lock and mechanically seamed standing seam?
faq.a: Snap-lock panels click together by hand over a clip and are suited to slopes of 3:12 and steeper. Mechanically seamed panels are folded together with a powered seamer, either a single 90 degree fold or a double 180 degree fold, and the double-lock version is weather-tight down to very low slopes. Mechanical seaming costs more in labor and is the right call for low slope, long panels, and heavy snow country.

faq.q: How much more does standing seam cost than a screw-down metal roof?
faq.a: In Northern Colorado, standing seam typically runs 40 to 70 percent more per square than an exposed-fastener panel roof on the same house. The premium pays for concealed clips, seamed joints, no field penetrations, and a finish and gauge that are usually higher spec. The exact gap varies by pitch, access, tear-off, decking condition, and how many flashings the roof needs.

faq.q: What gauge should a residential standing seam roof be?
faq.a: We specify 24 gauge steel on homes. It resists denting and oil canning far better than 26 gauge, and the cost difference on a whole roof is modest. 22 gauge shows up on commercial roofs and high-exposure mountain homes. Thinner 26 and 29 gauge panels belong on sheds and agricultural buildings, not on a roof you expect to last 50 years.

faq.q: Do I need snow guards on a standing seam roof in Colorado?
faq.a: On nearly every Colorado home, yes. Metal sheds snow in a single slab, and a slab off a 6:12 roof can tear off a gutter, crush a deck railing, or bury a gas meter. We lay out seam-clamped bar or fence retention in rows sized to the pitch, panel length, and local ground snow load, concentrated above entries, walkways, decks, and utilities. No holes are drilled through the panel.

faq.q: Can standing seam go on a low-slope or flat roof?
faq.a: A double-lock mechanically seamed panel with in-seam sealant can be installed on slopes as low as about 1:12, which makes it a long-term fix for low-slope commercial roofs that have been patched for years. Snap-lock cannot go that low. On very flat roofs with ponding, a membrane or a coating system is usually the better answer, and we will tell you which.

name: Slate Roofing
serviceType: Natural slate roof installation and repair
title: Slate Roofing Northern Colorado
description: Natural slate roofing in Northern Colorado: installation, repair, and restoration with copper flashings and a structural check. Get a free inspection.
lede: A natural slate roof is a stone shingle system that outlives the people who install it, when the framing can carry it and the flashings are made of metal that lasts as long as the stone. Here is what that takes in Colorado.
summary: Natural slate installation, slate-by-slate repair, and full restoration for historic homes and custom builds across Northern Colorado.

sections.h2: What a slate roof is, and what grade means
sections.html:
Roofing slate is quarried stone split along its natural cleavage into shingles roughly a quarter inch to three quarters of an inch thick, hung on nails with a headlap so every point on the roof has at least two layers of stone over it. It is the oldest roof covering still installed in North America, and the physics have not changed: the stone sheds water, the headlap keeps wind-driven rain out, and the nails and flashings hold it all together.

Slate is graded under ASTM C406 by water absorption and durability:

  • S1 (hard slate). Expected life of 75 years minimum, routinely 100 to 150 or more. Quarried in Vermont, New York, Virginia, and parts of Spain and Wales. This is what we specify for new work.
  • S2. 40 to 75 years. Acceptable on some repairs where matching an existing roof matters more than ultimate life.
  • S3. 20 to 40 years. Soft stone we do not install.

Standard thickness is a quarter inch. Heavy and estate-grade slates at half an inch to three quarters of an inch are specified for hail-prone exposures and for the look of a graduated roof, where thicker, larger slates at the eave step down to smaller ones at the ridge. Every slate is hung with copper or stainless nails, never galvanized, and valleys, step flashing, and chimney saddles are formed in 16 or 20 ounce copper or stainless steel, because a flashing that rusts out in 30 years makes no sense under stone that lasts 100.

sections.h2: Why slate suits Colorado, and where it does not
sections.html:
Weight comes first. Standard slate weighs 800 to 1,000 pounds per square and heavy slate runs 1,200 to 1,500. Add Larimer County design snow loads, which climb from 55 pounds per square foot on the plains to 110 at 8,000 feet, and the rafters, decking, and bearing walls have to be checked before any stone goes up. On a house built for asphalt, that review often ends with a structural engineer and sometimes with sistered rafters. We do not skip it.

Hail. This is the honest limitation. Thick, hard S1 slate stands up to most Front Range hail, but very large stones, the 2 inch and larger hail that hits Loveland, Fort Collins, and Greeley every few years, can crack individual slates. Slate has no UL 2218 Class 4 rating. Cracked slates are replaced one at a time, which is a repair, not a re-roof, but you want a contractor who can still do that work years later. If hail resistance on a budget is the goal, we will show you synthetic slate alongside the real thing.

Wildfire. Stone does not burn. Slate over a solid deck is a Class A assembly, which satisfies Colorado's Wildfire Resiliency Code in mapped wildland urban interface zones.

UV and freeze-thaw. Slate is unaffected by ultraviolet. Hard slate has such low water absorption that freeze-thaw does not split it, which is why 1890s slate roofs in Denver and Boulder are still in service.

Snow and ice. Snow does not slide off slate the way it does off metal, so ice dams are managed with a full membrane at eaves and valleys, ventilation, and pad-style snow guards above entries. The roof pitch also matters: slate wants 4:12 or steeper, and 6:12 and up is where it performs best.

sections.h2: Lifespan, maintenance, and why slate roofs actually fail
sections.html:
A hard slate roof fails from the metal, not the stone. Galvanized nails rust and let slates slide. Tin or galvanized valleys wear through. Chimney flashings crack at the mortar joints. On a 90 year old roof, the slate itself is usually fine and the roof is leaking because everything holding it has reached the end of its life.

Maintenance on a sound slate roof is an inspection every few years, from a ladder or with binoculars, for slipped, broken, or missing slates and for flashing condition, plus clearing debris from valleys. Walking a slate roof breaks slate, so anyone on it should be stepping on the headlap, not the exposed face, and using ladder hooks and roof ladders.

Three levels of work on an existing slate roof:

  1. Repair. Individual slates removed with a slate ripper and replaced on a copper bib or slate hook. Flashing patches. Done slate by slate and photographed.
  2. Restoration. Valleys, step flashing, and chimney saddles replaced in copper while the surrounding slate is lifted and reset.
  3. Re-lay. When nails or underlayment have failed across the roof, the slate is stripped, sorted, and re-hung on new underlayment with new copper flashings and nails. You keep the original stone and gain another century.

Before a sale, a slate roof should get a proper roof inspection from someone who knows what a cracked versus a weathered slate looks like, because a buyer's general inspector often cannot tell them apart.

sections.h2: What slate costs in Colorado
sections.html:
Slate is the most expensive roof covering we install. Typical installed ranges in Northern Colorado for new natural slate, including tear-off, full synthetic or felt underlayment, ice and water membrane, copper flashings, and copper nails:

  • Standard quarter inch S1 slate: roughly $2,000 to $2,800 per square
  • Heavy and architectural thicknesses: roughly $2,800 to $3,600 per square
  • Estate grade and graduated layouts: $3,600 to $4,000 per square and up

Repairs are priced per slate or per flashing, and a re-lay of existing stone usually lands well below new slate because the material is already on the roof. Structural upgrades, when the engineer calls for them, are a separate line item.

All of it varies by pitch, access, tear-off, decking, and detailing. Steep roofs over 8:12 add staging and slow the work. Multiple chimneys, dormers, and valleys mean more copper, and copper pricing moves. A slate roof is a 100 year decision, and the question to settle is whether the house and the owner are staying long enough to collect on it. We cover that math in Slate roofing: is it worth it?, and financing is available on qualifying projects.

sections.h2: Warranty: what to ask for in writing
sections.html:
Natural slate carries no manufacturer warranty in the way a shingle or a metal panel does. Some quarries and distributors will warrant their S1 slate against delamination or spalling for 50 to 100 years, and that document is worth having, but it covers the stone only. The nails, flashings, underlayment, and installation are on the contractor.

So the workmanship warranty is the whole conversation. Ask that it be written and specify:

  • The term in years, and whether it transfers to the next owner
  • That it covers slipped and broken slates caused by installation, not just leaks
  • That it covers flashing and penetration leaks with labor and materials
  • What metal was used for nails and flashings, by weight and alloy, listed in the contract
  • The slate source, grade, and thickness in writing, because a cheaper S2 slate looks identical on the pallet

For repairs on an existing roof, ask for before and after photos of each replaced slate and flashing. Every slate project starts with a walk-on free inspection and a written scope.

faq.q: Can my house support a slate roof?
faq.a: Many can, but it has to be confirmed. Standard slate weighs 8 to 10 pounds per square foot and heavy slate up to 15, several times what asphalt weighs, and Colorado snow load stacks on top of that. We evaluate the rafters, decking, and bearing, and bring in a structural engineer when the span, pitch, or elevation calls for it. If the structure cannot carry stone without major framing work, synthetic slate delivers the look at about a third of the weight.

faq.q: How does a slate roof hold up to Colorado hail?
faq.a: Thick, hard S1 slate resists most Front Range hail, and we specify heavier slate on exposures that see it often. Very large hail, 2 inches and up, can crack individual slates, which are replaced one at a time rather than re-roofing. Slate carries no Class 4 impact rating, so it does not qualify for impact-resistant insurance discounts. If hail is your main concern, we will quote Class 4 synthetic slate next to natural stone.

faq.q: Why is my slate roof leaking when the slates look fine?
faq.a: Almost always because the metal has failed before the stone. Galvanized nails rust and let slates slip, valleys and step flashings wear through, and chimney flashings open up at the mortar. On older roofs the slate often has 50 years left while the fasteners and flashings have none. The fix is a restoration or re-lay: new copper flashings and nails, with the original slate reset on new underlayment.

faq.q: How much does a slate roof cost in Colorado?
faq.a: Typical installed ranges in Northern Colorado run roughly $2,000 to $2,800 per square for standard quarter inch S1 slate and $2,800 to $4,000 or more for heavy, architectural, and graduated installations, with copper flashings and nails included. The number varies by pitch, access, tear-off, decking, and detailing, and any structural upgrades are separate. A re-lay of existing slate costs considerably less than new stone.

faq.q: Do you repair historic slate roofs?
faq.a: Yes. We match slate by source, color, size, and thickness, replace individual slates with copper bibs or hooks, and rebuild flashings in copper so they last as long as the stone. Where a home sits in a historic district, as in parts of Fort Collins and Boulder, we coordinate the scope with the preservation review so the repair matches what the certificate of appropriateness requires.

name: Tile Roofing
serviceType: Concrete and clay tile roof installation and repair
title: Tile Roofing Northern Colorado
description: Concrete and clay tile roofing in Northern Colorado: installation, tile lift and relay, underlayment replacement, hail repair. Get a free inspection.
lede: On a tile roof, the tile is the armor and the underlayment is the roof. Most tile problems in Colorado are underlayment and flashing problems, and most tile contractors who do not understand that end up replacing roofs that only needed a relay.
summary: Concrete and clay tile installation, lift and relay, underlayment replacement, and hail repair for stucco and Mediterranean-style homes in Northern Colorado.
lifespan: 50+ years for the tile; underlayment 20 to 30 years

sections.h2: What tile roofing is: concrete, clay, and the layers under them
sections.html:
A tile roof is a water-shedding system, not a waterproof one. Overlapping concrete or fired-clay tiles carry most of the rain and all of the sun and hail, but wind-driven rain and snowmelt are expected to get under them. The underlayment beneath, running from eave to ridge on the deck, is what actually keeps the house dry.

Concrete tile is a cast mix of sand, cement, and pigment, formed into flat, low-profile S, and high-barrel W profiles. It is freeze-thaw rated by nature, weighs 850 to 1,100 pounds per square (lightweight versions run 550 to 700), and is the most common tile around Loveland, Windsor, and Fort Collins.

Clay tile is fired, holds its color permanently, and comes in two-piece barrel and one-piece S shapes. It weighs 600 to 900 pounds per square depending on profile. For Colorado it must be ASTM C1167 Grade 1, the freeze-thaw grade. Grade 2 and 3 clay meant for the Southwest spalls and cracks after a few Front Range winters.

The layers that decide whether the roof lasts:

  • Underlayment. Two layers of ASTM D226 Type II felt, or a single self-adhered or high-temperature synthetic membrane rated for the service life of the tile, with ice and water membrane at eaves, valleys, and penetrations.
  • Battens. Elevated, drainable batten systems that let water and condensation leave the deck rather than sit against it.
  • Attachment. Nails, screws, clips, or foam adhesive by wind zone and pitch, with the field, perimeter, and ridge fastened differently.
  • Flashings. Pan and counter flashing at walls, crickets behind chimneys, and lead or malleable flashing at pipes. Most tile leaks start here.

sections.h2: Why tile suits Colorado, and what to plan for
sections.html:
Wildfire. Concrete and clay tile are non-combustible and form a Class A assembly, which meets the Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code requirement for mapped wildland urban interface parcels. The gap at the eave under barrel tile must be bird-stopped and ember-blocked, which code in WUI zones now requires.

UV and heat at altitude. Tile does not fade or chalk under high-altitude sun the way paint and asphalt do. The air space under the tile also keeps the deck cooler than any shingle roof, which lowers attic temperatures in July. The underlayment, however, bakes under that heat, which is why standard 15 pound felt fails in 15 to 20 years here and why we specify high-temperature membranes.

Hail. This is the limitation. Concrete tile chips and cracks under hail of about 1.5 inches and larger; clay fractures at similar sizes. Neither carries a UL 2218 Class 4 rating. After a Front Range storm the damage is often invisible from the ground and shows up as hairline cracks and chipped corners that let more water reach the underlayment. See hail damage roof repair for how we document that for a claim.

Snow load and weight. Full-weight tile at 900 to 1,100 pounds per square plus a 55 to 110 pound per square foot design snow load is a structural question. Switching a house from asphalt to tile requires a framing review, and lightweight concrete tile exists for exactly that situation.

Wind. Tile relies on fastening, not sealant, so the attachment schedule at eaves, rakes, and ridges follows the manufacturer's high-wind details for the 115 to 140 mph design speeds along the foothills.

sections.h2: Lifespan and maintenance: the underlayment clock
sections.html:
Concrete tile lasts 50 years or more and clay can go 75 to 100. Neither is the limiting factor. The underlayment is, and in Colorado's heat and dryness it typically reaches the end of its life at 20 to 30 years, sometimes less with original builder-grade felt.

The warning signs are a tile roof that leaks while the tiles look perfect, brittle or torn underlayment visible at the eave when a tile is lifted, and staining on the deck in the attic. The fix is a lift and relay: the tile is removed and stacked on the roof, the underlayment and flashings are replaced, and the original tile goes back down. You keep the look and skip the cost of new tile. On a 30 year old roof this is the single most common tile project we do.

Routine maintenance:

  • Walk the roof carefully (or let us) after any hail event and replace cracked and slipped tiles before water finds the underlayment
  • Keep valleys and the area behind chimneys clear of leaves and pine needles
  • Re-point or convert mortared ridges and hips to mechanically fastened ridge systems when the mortar starts to crumble
  • Check that bird stops and eave closures are intact

A tile roof should never be walked by anyone who does not know where to step. We include the condition of the underlayment, where it can be observed at the eave, in every free inspection.

sections.h2: What tile roofing costs in Colorado
sections.html:
Typical installed ranges in Northern Colorado, including tear-off of one shingle layer, high-temperature underlayment, battens, and standard flashings:

  • Concrete tile, flat and S profiles: roughly $1,000 to $1,700 per square
  • Clay tile, Grade 1, S and barrel profiles: roughly $1,500 to $2,500 per square
  • Lift and relay with new underlayment, reusing existing tile: roughly $500 to $900 per square
  • Individual tile replacement after hail: priced per tile plus access

Those numbers vary by pitch, access, tear-off, decking, and detailing. Two-piece barrel clay with mortared hips is the slow end of the labor scale. Discontinued profiles that have to be sourced from salvage add cost and lead time. A framing upgrade, when switching from asphalt to full-weight tile, is engineered and priced separately. If a hail storm is the reason you are here, see whether homeowners insurance covers roof replacement in Colorado before you decide between repair, relay, and replacement.

sections.h2: Warranty: what the tile covers and what it does not
sections.html:
Concrete and clay tile manufacturers commonly offer 50 year to lifetime limited warranties on the tile itself, usually covering manufacturing defects, freeze-thaw failure on properly graded tile, and sometimes color. Read the exclusions: hail, foot traffic, and improper installation are typically carved out, and the underlayment is not covered by the tile warranty at all.

Underlayment carries its own manufacturer warranty, often 20 to 30 years on premium high-temperature and self-adhered membranes, and a longer one on some systems when the whole assembly is installed per the manufacturer's tile specification. Ask which underlayment is in the bid, by product name, and what its warranty term is. A bid that says only "synthetic underlayment" is not telling you enough.

The workmanship warranty should cover leaks at flashings, penetrations, and ridges, tiles that slip or crack because they were fastened wrong, and labor and materials to fix them. Ask for the term in years, whether it transfers on sale, and whether it covers a lift-and-relay the same way it covers new installation.

faq.q: How long does a tile roof last in Colorado?
faq.a: The tile commonly lasts 50 years or more for concrete and longer for Grade 1 clay. The underlayment under it is what wears out, usually at 20 to 30 years in Colorado's heat and dryness, sometimes sooner with original builder-grade felt. Plan on at least one lift-and-relay during the life of the tile, and choose a high-temperature underlayment now to push that date out as far as possible.

faq.q: My tile roof is leaking but the tiles look fine. Why?
faq.a: Water is supposed to get under tile; the underlayment is supposed to carry it out. When the underlayment cracks, tears, or rots, or when a wall or chimney flashing fails, the leak shows up inside while the tile overhead looks perfect. The repair is a lift and relay of the affected area or the whole roof, replacing the underlayment and flashings and reinstalling the original tile.

faq.q: Does hail damage a tile roof?
faq.a: Yes. Hail of about 1.5 inches and larger chips and cracks concrete tile and fractures clay, and the damage is often invisible from the ground. Cracked tiles let more water reach the underlayment and shorten its life. We walk the roof, photograph every broken tile slope by slope, and give you a count and a repair-versus-relay-versus-replace recommendation you can hand to your adjuster.

faq.q: Can I put a tile roof on a house that has shingles now?
faq.a: Sometimes. Full-weight tile runs 850 to 1,100 pounds per square, several times what asphalt weighs, and Colorado snow load adds to it, so the framing has to be reviewed and an engineer involved when the spans are long. Where the structure cannot carry full-weight tile, lightweight concrete tile at roughly 550 to 700 pounds per square or synthetic tile are the usual answers.

faq.q: Can you match my existing tile for a repair?
faq.a: Usually. We identify the manufacturer and profile, then source matching or compatible tile from current production or salvage. On discontinued profiles we can often pull sound tiles from a rear or less visible slope to repair the slopes that face the street, then fill the rear slope with the closest available match. Color variation from decades of weathering is normal and fades with time.

name: Cedar Shake Roofing
serviceType: Cedar shake and shingle roof installation, repair, and replacement
title: Cedar Shake Roofing Colorado
description: Cedar shake roofing in Colorado: treated shake installation where code allows, repair, and Class A conversions in wildfire zones. Get a free inspection.
keywords: wood shake roof wildfire code colorado
lede: Cedar is a beautiful roof and a complicated one in Colorado. The wildfire code, the insurers, and the climate have all changed the rules. We install it where it is still allowed and tell you plainly where it is not.
summary: Treated cedar shake and shingle installation, repair, and cedar-to-Class A conversions, with straight answers on Colorado wildfire code and insurance.
lifespan: 20 to 30 years in Colorado with maintenance

sections.h2: What cedar shake roofing is
sections.html:
Cedar roofing comes in two forms. Shakes are split from the log, thick and rough-textured, and hung with a felt interlayment between courses to stop wind-driven rain. Shingles are sawn on both faces, thinner, smoother, and laid in a tighter pattern. Both come from western red cedar, graded by the industry bureau into Number 1 (Blue Label, 100 percent heartwood, 100 percent edge grain, no defects), Number 2, and Number 3. We only install Number 1 on a roof.

Cedar has to dry from both faces to last. The traditional assembly is spaced sheathing, skip boards with gaps that let air reach the underside, or solid decking with a ventilated batten layer over it. Fasteners are stainless or hot-dipped galvanized, because cedar's natural acids corrode electro-galvanized nails in a few years. Flashings are copper or heavy coated steel.

Fire-retardant treatment is the part of the conversation that matters most in Colorado. Pressure-impregnated shakes are tested as a Class B covering on their own, and as part of a specific assembly with a cap sheet or gypsum underlayment they can achieve Class A. Untreated cedar is Class C at best. The treatment is permanent in the sense that it is driven into the wood, but surface weathering slowly reduces its effectiveness over decades, and insurers know that.

sections.h2: Why cedar is a harder sell in Colorado than it used to be
sections.html:
Wildfire code. Colorado's Wildfire Resiliency Code was adopted in 2025 and has been enforced by local jurisdictions since July 2026. In mapped wildland urban interface zones, it requires a Class A roof covering or assembly, and on an existing building, replacing or repairing 25 percent or more of the roof covering triggers full compliance. Several mountain jurisdictions, including Boulder and Summit County, restricted wood roofs well before the state code. If your address is in a mapped zone, a new natural cedar roof is likely off the table, and even a large repair on an existing one may have to go Class A. We check the map before we quote.

Insurance. Many Colorado carriers surcharge wood roofs, cap them by age, or decline to write them. Ask your agent before you commit to cedar, and ask specifically about a treated Class A assembly, which some carriers accept.

Climate. Cedar lasts 40 years in the Pacific Northwest and 20 to 30 here. Low humidity and intense high-altitude UV dry the wood, cup and split the shakes, and open the keyways. Freeze-thaw works water into checks and spreads them. Hail splits shakes and dents them; cedar carries no Class 4 rating.

Snow and wind. Shakes hold snow rather than shedding it, which helps with ice management but means the roof carries full design snow load. Wind-lifted shakes are the most common storm repair we see on cedar in Loveland and Berthoud subdivisions built in the 1980s and 1990s.

None of this means cedar is wrong everywhere. On a Front Range lot outside the WUI map, with an insurer that will write it and an owner who will maintain it, treated Number 1 cedar is still a legitimate roof. See the best roofing materials for wildfire zones for the alternatives if it is not.

sections.h2: Lifespan and maintenance, and when to repair versus replace
sections.html:
Plan on 20 to 30 years from a well-installed, treated, maintained cedar roof in Colorado. The roof tells you where it is in that life:

  • Early and mid-life. Shakes weather to silver-gray. Occasional wind-lifted or split shakes are replaced individually. Moss and debris are cleared from keyways and valleys so the wood can dry.
  • Late life. Widespread cupping, shakes worn thin at the butt, exposed felt interlayment in the keyways, and leaks at the valleys and around penetrations. At this stage individual repairs stop paying for themselves.

Maintenance that actually extends a cedar roof: gentle debris removal (never pressure washing, which strips the surface), trimming trees back so the roof dries, keeping gutters clear, and replacing damaged shakes promptly. Surface-applied treatments and stains have mixed results and can void a fire-retardant rating, so ask before anyone sprays anything.

The repair-versus-replace question has a code dimension here that it does not have with other materials. If your address is in a mapped WUI zone and the repair would touch 25 percent or more of the roof, the code may require the whole covering to go Class A. We tell you where that line is before any work starts.

When replacement is the answer, the three paths are new treated cedar where allowed, synthetic shake that keeps the split-wood look with Class A and Class 4 ratings, and stone-coated steel shake profiles. Most cedar conversions in Northern Colorado now go synthetic.

sections.h2: What cedar shake roofing costs in Colorado
sections.html:
Typical installed ranges in Northern Colorado for Number 1 western red cedar, including tear-off, interlayment or ventilated batten assembly, stainless fasteners, and standard flashings:

  • Sawn cedar shingles: roughly $1,200 to $1,600 per square
  • Hand-split or taper-sawn shakes: roughly $1,300 to $1,700 per square
  • Fire-retardant treated shakes with a Class A assembly: add roughly $150 to $300 per square
  • Shake repair: priced per shake or per area, with access and flashing work itemized

Everything above varies by pitch, access, tear-off, decking, and detailing. Spaced sheathing that has to be converted to solid decking for a Class A assembly adds a line item. Cedar material pricing moves with lumber markets more than any other roof covering, so a quote is good for a defined period and we say what that period is.

For comparison, a Class A synthetic shake conversion usually lands in a similar range per square, and a Class 4 asphalt shake-look shingle well below it. We quote all three side by side so you can see what the cedar premium is buying. Financing is available on qualifying projects.

sections.h2: Warranty: what to ask for in writing
sections.html:
Cedar is a natural product, and material warranties reflect that. Treatment plants typically warrant fire-retardant shakes for the integrity of the treatment itself, often 20 to 30 years, and some producers warrant Number 1 grade against manufacturing defects. Neither covers weathering, splitting, hail, moss, or anything the climate does to wood, which is most of what happens to a cedar roof.

That puts the weight on the installation. Ask for a written workmanship warranty that states:

  • The term in years and whether it transfers
  • That it covers leaks at valleys, flashings, and penetrations with labor and materials
  • That it covers shakes that lift or slip because of fastening or exposure errors
  • The grade, treatment, and fastener type, listed in the contract so you can verify what was delivered
  • The Class A assembly components, if one was specified, with the listing number, because that document is what your insurer and your building department will ask for

If you are keeping an existing cedar roof, get a photo-documented free inspection with a shake count and a plain statement of remaining life. If you are replacing it after a storm, read our insurance claim roofing page before you call the carrier.

faq.q: Can I still get a cedar shake roof in Colorado?
faq.a: In many Front Range neighborhoods outside mapped wildland urban interface zones, yes, with fire-retardant treated Number 1 shakes and an insurer willing to write it. Inside a mapped WUI zone, the Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code requires a Class A covering or assembly, and several mountain jurisdictions restricted wood roofs before the state did. We check your parcel on the hazard map before we quote so there are no surprises at permit.

faq.q: Will my insurance cover a wood shake roof?
faq.a: It depends on the carrier. Some surcharge wood roofs, some write them only up to a certain age, and some decline them. A fire-retardant treated Class A assembly satisfies some carriers that will not write untreated cedar. Ask your agent in writing before you commit, and if the answer is no, a Class A synthetic shake usually resolves the problem while keeping the look.

faq.q: How long does a cedar roof last in Colorado?
faq.a: Plan on 20 to 30 years for a treated, well-installed, maintained Number 1 cedar roof here. Low humidity, high-altitude ultraviolet, freeze-thaw, and hail cup, split, and wear the shakes faster than in wetter, milder climates where cedar can reach 40 years. Keeping the roof clear of debris and trees so it can dry is the single biggest factor you control.

faq.q: Can you repair my cedar roof instead of replacing it?
faq.a: Often, yes. Split, cupped, and wind-lifted shakes can be replaced individually, and failed valleys and flashings can be rebuilt without disturbing sound shakes. The limits are the overall condition of the roof and the code: in a mapped WUI zone, repairing 25 percent or more of the covering can trigger a Class A requirement for the whole roof. We tell you where that line is before any work starts.

faq.q: What replaces cedar and still looks like it?
faq.a: Polymer synthetic shakes molded from real split cedar, which carry Class A fire and UL 2218 Class 4 impact ratings, weigh less than wood, and satisfy wildfire codes and most insurers. Stone-coated steel shake profiles are the other option, with the same ratings and a metal substrate. Both read as cedar from the street. We bring full-size samples so you can compare them against your existing roof.

name: Synthetic Roofing
serviceType: Synthetic slate and shake roof installation
h1: Synthetic Slate and Shake Roofing in Colorado
title: Synthetic Roofing Colorado
description: Synthetic roofing in Colorado: polymer slate and shake with Class 4 impact and Class A fire ratings at a third the weight of stone. Get a free inspection.
lede: Synthetic slate and shake give you the profile of stone or split cedar with a UL 2218 Class 4 impact rating, a Class A fire rating, and a weight most houses can carry without touching the framing. For a Colorado homeowner tired of hail claims, it is often the answer.
summary: Polymer slate and shake roofing with Class 4 impact and Class A fire ratings, installed on Front Range and mountain homes without structural upgrades.
lifespan: 50 years, with lifetime limited warranties common

sections.h2: What synthetic roofing is
sections.html:
Synthetic, or composite, roofing is a molded polymer tile, usually a virgin or recycled polyolefin or polyurethane blend with UV stabilizers and fire retardants mixed through the material, cast from molds taken off real slate and real hand-split cedar. The color goes all the way through the tile, so a chip or a scuff does not expose a different color underneath. Each tile nails to the deck like a shingle, with no mortar, clips, or specialty crews, over a standard synthetic underlayment.

Two product families:

  • Synthetic slate. Single-width or multi-width tiles that mimic quarried slate, offered in standard, graduated, and staggered layouts, with color blends that avoid the repeating look of early composites.
  • Synthetic shake. Tiles molded from split cedar, with the texture, taper, and random widths of the real thing. This is the usual replacement for a wood shake roof in a wildfire zone.

Weight is 250 to 400 pounds per square, compared to 800 to 1,500 for natural slate and 850 to 1,100 for concrete tile. That is in the same range as a heavy asphalt shingle, which means almost any house framed for shingles can carry synthetic without an engineer.

Not all synthetics are equal. Some products from the 2000s cracked and faded within a decade and gave the category a reputation. The current generation of leading lines has 15 to 25 years of Colorado installations to point to, and we only install products with an established record here, a Class 4 listing, and a Class A assembly listing.

sections.h2: Why synthetic suits Colorado
sections.html:
Hail. This is the headline. The products we install carry UL 2218 Class 4 ratings, the same 2 inch steel ball test used for impact-resistant shingles and metal, and the polymer flexes under impact where slate and tile crack. Many Colorado carriers discount premiums for Class 4 coverings; we provide the documentation. If you have filed a hail claim in Greeley, Windsor, or Loveland in the last decade, a Class 4 synthetic roof is how you stop filing them.

Wildfire. Synthetic shake and slate are tested as Class A assemblies, which is what the Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code requires in mapped wildland urban interface zones. That makes synthetic shake the most common cedar replacement in Estes Park, Nederland, and the Red Feather Lakes area. The tile itself is a plastic, so the Class A rating is for the listed assembly with its specified underlayment, and the installation has to follow it.

UV at altitude. The leading products are formulated with UV inhibitors through the full thickness of the tile, not just a surface coat, and warranted against fading and cracking. High-altitude sun is the hardest test these products face, and the ones with a Front Range track record have passed it.

Weight and snow load. At a quarter of the weight of stone, synthetic goes on houses that could never carry slate. In the mountains, that leaves the structure's full capacity for snow load rather than roof covering.

Wind. Synthetic tiles are nailed individually with a specified pattern and carry high-wind listings when fastened per the manufacturer's detail. They do not rely on a seal strip the way asphalt does, so cold-weather installation is not the problem it is with shingles.

HOAs. Architectural review boards that reject vertical metal panels generally approve synthetic slate and shake, because from the street it reads as the natural material. We bring full-size samples and photos of local installations to the review meeting.

sections.h2: Lifespan and maintenance
sections.html:
Leading synthetic products are warranted for 50 years or carry lifetime limited warranties, and the early-2000s installations from reputable lines are still in service on the Front Range with no fading or cracking that affects function. We treat 50 years as the planning number.

Maintenance is minimal. The tile does not absorb water, so moss and freeze-thaw are not issues. It does not shed granules, so gutters stay cleaner than they do under asphalt. What needs attention over time is the same list as any steep-slope roof: sealant at pipe boots and skylight curbs, flashings at walls and chimneys, and keeping valleys clear. A damaged tile, from a fallen limb or a dropped tool, is cut out and replaced individually without disturbing the neighbors.

The things to watch for when comparing products:

  • Color-through versus surface-coated tiles (surface coats wear and show)
  • A real UL 2218 Class 4 listing, not a "tested to" claim
  • A Class A listing for the assembly, with the underlayment named
  • Track record in Colorado specifically, because high-altitude UV is where weak formulations fail first

If you are weighing synthetic against the natural materials it imitates, the slate roofing and cedar shake roofing pages lay out what you give up and what you gain. The short version: you give up the texture up close and the century of lifespan on hard slate, and you gain hail resistance, fire rating, and a weight your house can carry.

sections.h2: What synthetic roofing costs in Colorado
sections.html:
Typical installed ranges in Northern Colorado, including tear-off of one shingle layer, synthetic underlayment, ice and water membrane at eaves and valleys, and standard flashings:

  • Synthetic shake: roughly $1,100 to $1,700 per square
  • Synthetic slate, standard layout: roughly $1,200 to $1,800 per square
  • Synthetic slate, multi-width or graduated layout: roughly $1,500 to $2,000 per square

That puts synthetic above Class 4 asphalt shingles, in the same range as standing seam metal, and well below natural slate or clay tile. The ranges vary by pitch, access, tear-off, decking, and detailing. A staggered or graduated slate layout takes longer to lay than a straight course. Steep roofs add staging. Mountain homes add full-deck high-temperature membrane and snow retention designed for a textured surface.

On a hail-driven replacement, the insurance settlement typically covers like-kind replacement of the existing roof, and the owner pays the difference to upgrade to synthetic. Read our guide to Class 4 roofs and Colorado insurance discounts to see how the premium reduction offsets that upgrade over time, and ask about financing on qualifying projects.

sections.h2: Warranty: what to ask for in writing
sections.html:
Synthetic manufacturers typically offer 50 year or lifetime limited material warranties, which is a stronger document than natural slate, cedar, or tile can offer. Read what "limited" means in the one you are handed. Common structure: full material replacement for an initial period, often 10 years, then prorated coverage for the balance. Some add labor coverage for the first years, and some require the installer to be certified by the manufacturer for the full warranty to apply. Fading, cracking, and freeze-thaw are usually covered; hail is sometimes covered under a separate impact provision and sometimes excluded, so ask that question directly.

The workmanship warranty should cover leaks at flashings, penetrations, valleys, and ridges, and tiles that lift or crack because of fastening errors, with labor and materials. Ask for the term in years, whether it transfers to a buyer, and who services it.

Also get in writing:

  • The product name, profile, and color blend
  • The underlayment, by product, so the Class A assembly listing is traceable
  • The Class 4 listing number for your insurance file
  • The fastening pattern used, because wind coverage depends on it

A free inspection with samples on your roof is the right first step.

faq.q: Is synthetic slate really hail resistant?
faq.a: The products we install carry UL 2218 Class 4 ratings, the highest impact class, earned by surviving a 2 inch steel ball dropped from 20 feet without cracking. The polymer flexes where natural slate and concrete tile fracture. Class 4 is also the rating most Colorado carriers discount, and we supply the listing documentation for your agent. Very large hail can still scuff a tile, but scuffs on a color-through tile are cosmetic.

faq.q: How long does a synthetic roof last?
faq.a: Leading synthetic slate and shake products carry 50 year or lifetime limited warranties, and installations from the early 2000s are still performing on the Front Range under high-altitude sun. We plan on 50 years. The caveat is product selection: older or budget composites cracked and faded within a decade, so we only install lines with a documented Colorado track record and color-through, UV-stabilized construction.

faq.q: Does synthetic slate look fake?
faq.a: Up close, a trained eye can tell. From the curb, with a multi-width layout, a proper color blend, and tiles molded from real slate or split cedar, most people cannot, and HOA review boards routinely approve it where they reject metal panels. We bring full-size samples and show you local installations so you judge it on a roof, not in a brochure.

faq.q: Can synthetic shake replace my cedar roof in a wildfire zone?
faq.a: Yes. Class A rated synthetic shake is the most common replacement for wood shake roofs in Colorado's mapped wildland urban interface zones, where the Wildfire Resiliency Code requires a Class A covering or assembly. It keeps the split-wood look, weighs less than cedar, and satisfies most insurers that will not write wood. The Class A rating applies to the listed assembly, so the underlayment and installation have to follow the manufacturer's specification.

faq.q: How much does synthetic roofing cost compared to real slate?
faq.a: Installed synthetic slate in Northern Colorado typically runs roughly $1,200 to $2,000 per square, compared to roughly $2,000 to $4,000 for natural slate, and synthetic needs no structural upgrade on most homes. It costs more than Class 4 asphalt and about the same as standing seam metal. Those figures vary by pitch, access, tear-off, decking, and layout, and a written itemized estimate is the only real comparison.

name: Roof Coatings
serviceType: Fluid-applied roof coating and restoration systems
title: Roof Coatings Northern Colorado
description: Roof coatings in Northern Colorado: silicone, acrylic, and urethane systems for flat and low-slope commercial roofs, survey first. Get a free inspection.
lede: A coating system can add 10 to 20 years to a sound low-slope roof for a fraction of replacement cost. The same coating over a wet roof is the most expensive paint job you will ever buy. The moisture survey is what tells the difference, and it comes first.
summary: Silicone, acrylic, and urethane coating systems for flat, low-slope, and metal commercial roofs, specified after a moisture survey and adhesion testing.

sections.h2: What a roof coating system is
sections.html:
A roof coating is a fluid-applied, seamless membrane installed over an existing roof to stop leaks, reflect sun, and extend service life without a tear-off. It is a system, not a bucket of paint: cleaning, repair of wet or failed areas, reinforcement of every seam and penetration, a primer where the substrate needs it, and then a base and top coat applied to a specified thickness and measured in mils. The three chemistries we install:

  • Silicone. Moisture-cured, stays flexible, and does not break down under standing water. The default for flat roofs with ponding. It picks up dirt over time and is hard to recoat with anything other than silicone.
  • Acrylic. Water-based, lowest cost, highly reflective, and easy to recoat. It erodes under ponding water and needs a roof with positive drainage and a dry window to cure.
  • Urethane (polyurethane). The toughest film, with the best impact and foot-traffic resistance. Common as a base coat under silicone on roofs with hail exposure or rooftop equipment traffic, and on metal.

Substrates we coat: aged TPO and EPDM single-ply, modified bitumen, built-up roofing, spray polyurethane foam, and metal (R-panel and standing seam) after rust treatment and fastener sealing. We do not coat asphalt shingles, and we will explain why if anyone has offered to.

Thickness is the product. A 10 year silicone warranty typically requires about 30 mils applied, a 15 year about 35, and a 20 year about 40, and the manufacturer verifies it with wet-film gauges and sometimes core samples. A bid that does not state a mil thickness is not specifying a system.

sections.h2: Why coatings suit Colorado commercial roofs
sections.html:
UV at altitude. Front Range sun is the main thing that ages a single-ply or modified bitumen roof: it chalks the surface, embrittles the membrane, and opens seams. A white silicone or acrylic coating reflects most of that solar load, drops rooftop surface temperatures by tens of degrees in summer, reduces thermal cycling on the membrane underneath, and lowers cooling cost on the floor below. On a 40,000 square foot warehouse in Fort Collins or Greeley, that is real money.

Hail. A coating is only as hail-resistant as the roof under it. A urethane base coat adds impact resistance and some systems carry impact listings, but large hail that would split an aged membrane will damage a coating over it. On a roof that has already taken hail, the moisture survey and a storm damage assessment come before any coating conversation.

Freeze-thaw and ponding. Flat roofs in Colorado pond at drains and scuppers and then freeze. Silicone tolerates that cycle; acrylic does not. Where ponding is chronic, we look at whether tapered insulation, added drains, or crickets can fix the water problem rather than just coating over it.

Wind and the building envelope. A coating does not change the roof's uplift resistance. If a single-ply roof is losing adhesion or fasteners are backing out, that gets fixed first, because a coating over a loose membrane fails with it.

Snow in the mountains. Low-slope roofs in Winter Park and Steamboat hold deep snow all winter and the application window is short, but silicone restoration over sound metal and single-ply is a long-term fix for mountain commercial buildings that get patched every spring.

sections.h2: Lifespan, maintenance, and when a coating is the wrong answer
sections.html:
Manufacturer systems are warranted for 10, 15, or 20 years depending on the chemistry and the mil thickness applied. At the end of that term, a sound coating is cleaned and recoated at a fraction of the original cost, with no tear-off, which is the real value of the system over a roof's life.

Maintenance is an annual inspection and a cleaning as needed: debris at drains, sealant at penetrations added since the coating went on, and a check for mechanical damage from rooftop trades. Any new HVAC curb or conduit cut into a coated roof needs to be flashed into the system, not just caulked.

When a coating is the wrong answer, and we will say so:

  • More than about a quarter of the insulation is wet. Wet insulation has to be cut out and replaced before coating, and past a certain percentage, replacement is cheaper.
  • The membrane is at the end of its life: brittle, shattered seams, shrinkage pulling at the perimeter.
  • The roof deck is damaged or the structure is deflecting.
  • It is a shingle roof. Shingle coatings trap moisture, void warranties, and do not perform.

Every coating quote starts with an infrared or nuclear moisture survey, core samples where the survey flags wet areas, and field adhesion pull tests on the actual substrate. The findings go in a written report, and a commercial roof inspection on its own is available when a board or lender needs the condition documented first.

sections.h2: What roof coatings cost in Colorado
sections.html:
Coatings are priced per square foot of roof, not per square. Typical installed ranges in Northern Colorado for a complete system on a sound substrate, including cleaning, seam and penetration reinforcement, and the specified mil thickness:

  • Acrylic system, 10 year: roughly $2.00 to $3.50 per square foot
  • Silicone system, 10 to 20 year: roughly $2.50 to $4.50 per square foot
  • Urethane base with silicone top, or metal roof restoration with rust treatment and fastener sealing: roughly $3.50 to $5.50 per square foot

Replacement of wet insulation and membrane, where the survey finds it, is priced separately per square foot of affected area. Tapered insulation or added drains to correct ponding are their own line items.

All of it varies by substrate, condition, roof size, access, the number of penetrations and curbs, and the warranty term selected, since a 20 year system uses roughly a third more material than a 10 year one. For comparison, a tear-off and new single-ply roof in this market generally runs several times the per-square-foot cost of a coating system on the same building. We quote both so your board or owner can compare on one page, and our post on coatings for flat commercial roofs walks through a sample comparison.

sections.h2: Warranty: manufacturer system versus contractor
sections.html:
Coating warranties come in two very different forms, and the difference is worth understanding before you sign.

Material-only warranty. The manufacturer warrants the product against defects. It does not cover leaks or labor. This is what you get when a contractor buys product and applies it without manufacturer involvement.

System (labor and material) warranty. The manufacturer approves the contractor, reviews the moisture survey and adhesion tests, may inspect during and after application, and then issues a warranty that covers leaks for 10, 15, or 20 years with labor and material. This requires the specified mil thickness, the specified seam and penetration details, and documentation. It is the warranty worth paying for on a commercial building, and the one a property manager should insist on.

The contractor's workmanship warranty covers the gap: application errors, missed seams, and penetrations that were not detailed, for a stated term with labor and materials.

Ask for, in writing:

  • The manufacturer, product, and system name
  • The mil thickness and how it will be verified
  • The warranty type (material-only or system), the term, and whether it is transferable
  • The moisture survey and adhesion test results
  • What annual maintenance the warranty requires to stay in force

A free inspection with a moisture survey is where every coating project starts.

faq.q: How much does a roof coating cost compared to replacement?
faq.a: A complete coating system in Northern Colorado typically runs roughly $2.00 to $5.50 per square foot depending on chemistry, substrate, and warranty term, while a tear-off and new single-ply or modified bitumen roof on the same building generally costs several times that. The gap narrows when a lot of wet insulation has to be replaced first, which is why the moisture survey comes before the quote. We price both so you can compare.

faq.q: Can you coat a roof that has ponding water?
faq.a: Yes, with silicone, which cures by moisture and holds up under standing water indefinitely. Acrylic erodes under ponding and is the wrong product for that roof. We also look at whether the ponding itself can be corrected with tapered insulation, crickets, or added drains, because water that sits on a roof is still a load, a freeze-thaw cycle, and a leak risk at every penetration it reaches.

faq.q: Will a coating fix my leaks?
faq.a: If the leaks come from aged seams, pinholes, cracked flashings, and open penetrations on a roof whose insulation and deck are still sound, yes, because those are exactly what seam reinforcement and a seamless membrane address. If the insulation is saturated or the deck is damaged, those areas have to be cut out and replaced first, or the coating traps the water and the leak comes back. The moisture survey tells us which situation you have.

faq.q: Can you coat a shingle roof?
faq.a: No, and we recommend walking away from anyone who offers to. Coatings on asphalt shingles trap moisture under the shingle, void the shingle manufacturer's warranty, and do not extend the roof's life in any meaningful way. Shingle roofs are repaired or replaced. Coatings belong on low-slope membrane roofs, spray foam, and metal, where there is a continuous substrate for the film to bond to.

faq.q: How long does a roof coating last?
faq.a: Manufacturer system warranties run 10, 15, or 20 years, set by the chemistry and the mil thickness applied, roughly 30 mils for a 10 year silicone system and 40 mils for 20 years. Silicone generally outlasts acrylic in Colorado's UV and ponding conditions. At the end of the term, a sound coating is cleaned and recoated without a tear-off, which is where the long-term value of the system comes from.

sections.h2: What commercial roofing covers
sections.html:
Commercial roofing is mostly low-slope work: membrane and built-up systems on retail, office, warehouse, medical, and multifamily buildings where the pitch is too flat for shingles to shed water. It also includes steep-slope work on clubhouses and townhome rows, and the metal retrofits that go over aging panel roofs on industrial and agricultural buildings. The systems we install and service:

  • TPO (thermoplastic polyolefin): a white, heat-welded single-ply membrane. The most common new low-slope roof in Colorado today because it is reflective, weldable, and cost-effective.
  • EPDM: black synthetic rubber, fully adhered or mechanically fastened, with taped seams. Flexible in cold and proven over decades, but seams and adhesives are the weak point.
  • PVC: a heat-welded thermoplastic with stronger seams and better chemical resistance than TPO. The right call over restaurants and anything venting grease.
  • Modified bitumen: asphalt sheets reinforced with polyester or fiberglass, torched, cold-applied, or self-adhered in two or three plies. Tough underfoot and forgiving of rooftop traffic.
  • Metal retrofit: new standing seam panels or a membrane installed over an existing metal roof using sub-framing or flute fill, which keeps the building open during the work.
  • Coatings: silicone, acrylic, or urethane over a sound existing roof to add years before replacement. Our roof coatings page covers when that is the right answer and when it is throwing money at wet insulation.

sections.h2: Why Colorado is hard on flat roofs
sections.html:
Hail on membranes. A single-ply sheet over rigid polyiso has nothing underneath to absorb an impact. Large hail fractures the insulation facer and can puncture the membrane outright, and the damage often shows up as a scatter of leaks months later. A heavier membrane (60 or 80 mil instead of 45), a cover board between the insulation and the sheet, and fleece-backed membranes all change how a roof survives a June storm. We spec them and tell you what each one adds to the number.

UV at altitude. At 5,000 feet the UV index runs well above sea level. UV is what turns membranes chalky and brittle and dries the plasticizers out of older PVC. Reflective white roofs age slower and cut summer cooling loads, but they show every scuff and ponding ring.

Snow load and drainage. Flat roofs do not shed snow. A wet March storm can leave 20 to 30 pounds per square foot on the deck, and drifting against parapets and rooftop units doubles that locally. Roofs with clogged drains, dead-level decks, or sag between joists hold water after the melt, and ponding water is the fastest way to kill any membrane. We check drain and scupper capacity, add tapered insulation or crickets where water sits, and flag structural concerns before they become a collapse conversation.

Wind. Downslope winds off the foothills top 80 mph several times a winter. On a low-slope roof the failure point is the perimeter and corners, where uplift is highest. Fastening density, edge metal rated to ANSI/SPRI ES-1, and properly terminated parapet flashings are what keep a membrane on the building.

sections.h2: Property managers and HOAs: how we run the job
sections.html:
Commercial work succeeds or fails on logistics, not on the membrane brand. What to expect from us on every project:

  • Phasing. Occupied buildings and multifamily communities are roofed in sections so tenants keep parking, deliveries keep moving, and nothing is left open overnight. You get a phasing plan with dates before mobilization.
  • Certificates of insurance. General liability and workers' compensation certificates naming the owner or association as additional insured, delivered before anyone is on the roof. A bidder who cannot produce one on request has told you something.
  • Safety plan. A site-specific fall protection plan, warning lines, and controlled access zones. An injury on your property is your problem too.
  • Board-ready documentation. A photo record of every phase, a written scope that matches the proposal line by line, and a close-out package your management company can file with the reserve study.
  • Maintenance programs. Semi-annual inspections, drain clearing, seam and flashing checks, and a written condition report with photos. Most manufacturer warranties require documented maintenance to stay in force, and a maintenance file is also what proves a hail claim was a storm and not neglect. See roof inspections for what the report includes.

Where a 40-plus-year roof makes more sense than another membrane cycle, we also install standing seam metal on commercial and HOA buildings.
