sections.h2: What commercial roofing costs in Colorado
sections.html: Low-slope pricing is quoted per square (100 square feet) and swings far more than residential shingle work. A mechanically fastened 60 mil TPO recover over an existing roof lands in a very different range than a full tear-off with new tapered polyiso, cover board, and a fully adhered membrane. The variables that move the number: whether the existing roof can stay (code allows at most two layers), wet insulation found by core cuts or infrared scan, the R-value required by the current energy code, parapet height and edge metal, the count of curbs, drains, and penetrations, and crane or lift access. We give you a line-item proposal with unit prices for deck replacement and wet insulation so change orders are not a surprise. Costs vary by building, system, and season. Request a proposal and we will walk the roof first.

sections.h2: Warranties and what to get in writing
sections.html: Commercial roofs carry two warranties, and the difference matters. The manufacturer warranty covers the membrane and, on a full system warranty, the insulation, fasteners, and flashings, typically for 10 to 25 years. A no-dollar-limit (NDL) system warranty is the one worth having; it requires an approved installer, a manufacturer inspection at completion, and a maintenance record. A material-only warranty covers the sheet and nothing else. The workmanship warranty comes from the contractor and covers installation defects: seams, flashings, terminations, and leaks caused by the work. Get both in writing with the term, what voids them, transfer provisions if the building sells, and whether hail is excluded, which on most manufacturer warranties it is. Ask every bidder the same list and compare the answers in writing.

faq.q: What is the best flat roof material for Colorado hail?
faq.a: For most buildings, a 60 or 80 mil TPO or PVC membrane over a cover board is the best balance of hail resistance and cost. The cover board is the part people skip; it spreads the impact so hail bruises the board instead of fracturing the insulation facer. A granulated modified bitumen cap sheet also performs well. Where budget allows, a standing seam metal retrofit outlasts every membrane, but confirm how your policy treats cosmetic denting.

faq.q: Can you install a new roof over my existing commercial roof?
faq.a: Often, yes. Code allows a recover over one existing roof if the insulation is dry and the deck is sound, and it saves tear-off and disposal cost. We confirm with core cuts or an infrared moisture scan first. Wet insulation under a new membrane rots the deck and voids the warranty, so a recover over a wet roof is not a savings, it is a deferred tear-off at a higher price.

faq.q: How often should a commercial roof be inspected in Colorado?
faq.a: Twice a year, spring and fall, plus after any hail or high-wind event. Spring catches winter damage and clears drains before monsoon season; fall clears leaves and checks seams before freeze-thaw cycling. Most manufacturer system warranties require documented inspections to stay in force, and the maintenance file is what separates a covered storm claim from a denied wear-and-tear claim.

faq.q: Do you provide certificates of insurance for HOA and commercial projects?
faq.a: Yes. We carry general liability and workers' compensation and provide certificates naming the owner, association, or management company as additional insured before mobilization. We also supply a site-specific safety plan on request. If a bidder hesitates to produce a certificate, assume the coverage is thin or does not exist, because an uninsured injury on your roof becomes your claim.

faq.q: How long does a commercial re-roof take?
faq.a: It depends on square footage, tear-off, and weather. A single-story retail building might take a week; a multifamily community phased around residents can run several weeks. We never open more roof than we can dry in the same day, because a Front Range afternoon storm does not care about the schedule. Your proposal includes a phasing plan with dates, and we update it in writing if weather moves it.

sections.h2: What roof repair covers
sections.html:
Nearly every residential leak traces back to one of a handful of details, and almost none of them are in the middle of a shingle field. The repairs we do most:

  • Leak diagnosis. We start in the attic when there is one, follow the stain to the entry point, then go on the roof and water-test if the source is not obvious. Guessing from the ground and caulking everything in sight is not a repair.
  • Flashing. Chimney step and counter flashing, roof-to-wall transitions, skylight curbs, and kick-out flashing where a roof edge meets siding. Flashing failures account for more leaks than any other single cause.
  • Pipe boots. The rubber collar on a plumbing vent cracks after 8 to 12 years in Colorado sun. It is a 30-minute fix that, left alone, rots a bay of decking.
  • Valleys. Open metal valleys corrode or lift; closed-cut valleys wear through where two slopes dump water in one trough.
  • Wind-lifted shingles. Creased, lifted, and missing shingles replaced and hand-sealed, with the surrounding field checked for broken seals that will go in the next storm.
  • Ice dam damage. Repair of water-damaged decking and underlayment at the eaves, plus the ventilation and air-sealing fixes that stop the dam from forming again.
  • Emergency dry-in. Tarping and temporary patches to stop active water intrusion until a permanent repair can be scheduled.

sections.h2: Why Colorado roofs fail where they do
sections.html:
The same roof detail that lasts 20 years in Portland lasts 10 on the Front Range, and the reasons are specific.

UV at altitude cooks the rubber in pipe boots, the sealant on exposed nail heads, and the asphalt binder in shingles. Boots split, sealant shrinks and pulls away, shingles get brittle and crack when a tech walks on them in February.

Thermal cycling on a Colorado winter day can swing 50 degrees between dawn and afternoon. Metal flashing expands and contracts against sealant that cannot keep up, and the joint opens a hairline at a time.

Wind off the foothills breaks shingle seal strips, especially on the west and northwest slopes and along rakes and ridges. A shingle that has been lifted once rarely re-seals, so it creases and tears in the next event.

Ice dams form when attic heat melts snow on the upper roof and it refreezes at the cold eave. Water backs up under the shingles. Ice and water shield at the eaves is required by code for exactly this reason, and older roofs often do not have it.

Hail bruises shingles without opening them, and the leak shows up a year or two later when the fractured mat finally lets go. If your roof has been through a documented storm, a hail damage inspection should come before any repair estimate, because the right answer may be a claim rather than a patch.

sections.h2: Repair or replace: how we make the call
sections.html:
A repair is the right answer when the roof has meaningful life left, the damage is confined to a detail or a slope, and matching material is available. A replacement is the right answer when any of these are true:

  • The roof is within a few years of the end of its expected life and the repair would be the first of many.
  • Granule loss is widespread, shingles are cupping or cracking across the field, or the mat shows through.
  • Decking is soft in multiple areas, which usually means the underlayment failed long ago.
  • Storm damage is spread across most slopes and your insurer owes a replacement, not a patch.
  • The original shingle is discontinued and a repair would leave an obvious mismatch that hurts resale.

We put the age, the condition photos, and both numbers in writing so you can decide. A full replacement with Class 4 shingles sometimes costs less over ten years than a roof that gets repaired after every storm, and sometimes it does not. Our guide on how long a roof lasts in Colorado walks through the math.

sections.h2: What roof repairs cost in Colorado
sections.html: Every roofer carries a service-call minimum, because getting a crew, a ladder, and materials to a roof costs the same whether the fix takes 20 minutes or two hours. On the Front Range that minimum typically covers a single pipe boot, a few wind-lifted shingles, or resealing an exposed flashing. Chimney reflashing, valley rebuilds, skylight curb repairs, and decking replacement run into the low thousands depending on access, roof pitch, material, and how much tear-back is needed to do it right. Slate, tile, and metal repairs cost more than asphalt because the material and the labor are specialized. We give you a written, itemized price before the work starts, and the before-and-after photos when it ends. Costs vary by roof; schedule an inspection and we will show you what we find.

sections.h2: Warranty on repairs and what to ask for
sections.html: A repair should come with a written workmanship warranty that covers the specific detail that was fixed, for a stated term, against leaks caused by the work. Ask for that in writing with the repair location described, because a vague "one year on labor" is hard to enforce when the roof has three other aging details nearby. Manufacturer warranties on the original shingles usually do not cover repairs by a different installer, and they never cover storm damage, so do not expect a repair to extend the shingle warranty. What a good repair does is match the manufacturer's installation requirements so the fix does not create a new problem. We document every repair with photos and the materials used, and you keep that file for resale or a future claim.

faq.q: Why is my roof leaking when it is not raining?
faq.a: In Colorado winters the usual answer is an ice dam or attic condensation. Snow melts on the warm upper roof, refreezes at the eave, and the pooled water backs up under the shingles and drips on sunny afternoons. Condensation happens when warm, moist house air reaches a cold roof deck through gaps in the ceiling. Both are fixed with air sealing, insulation, and ventilation, not with more caulk on the shingles.

faq.q: Can you repair just the damaged part of a roof?
faq.a: Yes, when the damage is confined to one detail or slope and matching shingles are available. We replace the damaged shingles, hand-seal them, and check the surrounding field for broken seals. When damage runs across most of the roof, a partial repair leaves you with a patchwork that fails piece by piece, and if a storm caused it, your insurer may owe a full replacement instead.

faq.q: How much does a roof repair cost in Colorado?
faq.a: Most roofers charge a service-call minimum that covers small fixes like a pipe boot or a few lifted shingles. Flashing rebuilds, valley repairs, and decking replacement run higher, typically into the low thousands, and specialty materials cost more than asphalt. The honest answer depends on access, pitch, and how much has to come apart to fix the real source. We put the itemized price in writing before any work starts.

faq.q: Should I repair or replace a 15-year-old asphalt roof?
faq.a: It depends on condition, not age alone. A 15-year-old architectural shingle roof with intact granules and one failed flashing is worth repairing. The same roof with widespread granule loss, cracking, or soft decking is near the end of its life on the Front Range, where UV and hail shorten shingle life, and money spent on repairs is better put toward replacement. We photograph the condition and give you both numbers.

faq.q: Do you do emergency roof repairs?
faq.a: Yes. For active leaks we prioritize a same-day or next-day dry-in: tarping, temporary patching, and stopping water from reaching the interior. The permanent repair follows once the roof is dry and we have traced the source. Keep photos of the interior damage and the emergency work, because if the cause was a storm, those photos and the mitigation invoice are part of your insurance claim.

sections.h2: How hail damages each roofing material
sections.html:
Hail does not damage every roof the same way, and knowing what to look for on your material is the difference between catching a claim and finding a rotten deck three years later.

  • Asphalt shingles. The impact knocks granules off and bruises the fiberglass mat underneath. A fresh hit feels soft, like a bruise on fruit, and the exposed asphalt looks black and shiny. The mat is fractured even when the surface looks intact, and UV finishes the job over the next year or two until the shingle leaks.
  • Metal. Steel and aluminum panels dent rather than puncture. The roof still sheds water, which is why many policies carry a cosmetic damage exclusion for metal. Functional damage, such as dents that break the paint and start corrosion, crushed seams, or split fasteners, is a different matter, and heavier-gauge panels resist both.
  • Concrete and clay tile. Tile cracks at edges and corners and breaks along the water channel. A cracked tile may look fine from the ground and funnel water straight onto an underlayment that is already 25 years old.
  • Cedar shake. Hail splits shakes along the grain and knocks out the softer wood between the growth rings. Splits open wider with every freeze-thaw cycle.
  • Low-slope membranes. Hail fractures the insulation under TPO and EPDM and can puncture thinner sheets outright. Damage shows as a scatter of leaks after the next heavy rain.

sections.h2: Colorado hail: when it comes and how big it gets
sections.html: The Front Range hail season runs from May through August with the peak in June, when afternoon storms build over the foothills and drift east across Loveland, Fort Collins, Greeley, and the I-25 corridor. National insurer and claims data consistently put Colorado in the top three to five states for hail claims and hail losses, with hundreds of thousands of claims and hundreds of millions of dollars in a bad year. Hail one inch in diameter, about the size of a quarter, is enough to bruise standard asphalt shingles. Golf-ball hail breaks tile and splits cedar. Anything larger punches through aging roofs of every type. Most Front Range homes will see at least one damaging storm in the life of the roof, which is why we treat Class 4 impact resistance as the default spec here rather than an upgrade. Our guide on how to tell if your roof has hail damage covers what you can check from the ground before you call.

sections.h2: How we inspect and document hail damage
sections.html:
A hail inspection is a documentation job. The adjuster who comes later will use the same method, and if our findings do not hold up to it, they are worthless to you.

  1. Collateral damage first. Soft metals tell the story: dented gutters, downspouts, roof vents, AC condenser fins, window screens, and the painted metal on fences and mailboxes. If the soft metals are clean, the roof probably is too, and we tell you that.
  2. Test squares. We chalk a 10 foot by 10 foot square on each slope, mark every hail hit inside it, and count. Insurers generally look for a threshold of hits per square per slope to justify replacing that slope, and the count is what settles the argument.
  3. Slope-by-slope photos. Wide shots to show the pattern, close-ups with a chalk circle and a scale reference on individual hits, and photos of the directional pattern (hail usually damages the slopes facing the storm hardest).
  4. Measurement. Roof dimensions, pitch, layers, and penetrations, so the scope can be priced accurately.
  5. Written report. Findings, photos, and a plain recommendation: repair, claim, or leave it alone. You keep it either way.

sections.h2: What happens after the storm, and how fast
sections.html:
Day one. Photograph anything dented or broken on the ground, note the date and time of the storm, and move vehicles if more weather is coming. Do not get on the roof.

First week. Get a real inspection. Door knockers will arrive within hours of a big storm; the ones you want are the ones with a Loveland address you can drive past. Read what to do after a hail storm before you sign anything.

Filing. If the damage is there, you file the claim with your carrier. Most policies set a deadline from the date of loss to report, and waiting makes the damage harder to tie to a specific storm, so file promptly.

Adjuster meeting. Typically one to three weeks after filing. Once you have signed a contract with us, we meet the adjuster on your roof to walk the test squares and point out what we documented.

Build. Materials order, permit, and the roof itself, usually one to two days for a typical home. Colorado law gives you at least a year to complete the work and collect recoverable depreciation on most policies, so there is no need to rush into a bad contract. The claim mechanics are on our insurance claim roofing page.

sections.h2: Class 4 upgrades and what repair or replacement costs
sections.html:
UL 2218 Class 4 is the top impact rating for roofing. To earn it, a product takes a 2-inch steel ball dropped from 20 feet, twice in the same spot, without cracking through to the back of the material. Class 4 asphalt shingles use a modified polymer formulation or a reinforced mat; metal and many synthetic products earn the rating as well. Many Colorado insurers offer a premium discount for a Class 4 roof, and Fort Collins requires Class 4 asphalt shingles on new and replacement roofs. Our post on Class 4 shingles and insurance discounts explains how to ask your agent.

Cost depends on whether a claim is involved. When your insurer approves a replacement, your cost is your deductible plus any upgrade you choose, such as the difference between a standard architectural shingle and Class 4. When the damage falls short of a claim, repair pricing starts at a service-call minimum and scales with the number of slopes affected. Replacement outside a claim is priced per square and varies by material, roof size, pitch, layers, and decking condition. We quote both options in writing side by side.

sections.h2: Warranty after a hail repair or replacement
sections.html: Manufacturer warranties on roofing materials exclude hail damage almost without exception; the warranty covers manufacturing defects, not weather. A Class 4 rating is a test result, not a guarantee the roof will never be damaged. What you should get in writing: the manufacturer's material warranty registered in your name, the contractor's workmanship warranty with its term and what it covers, and a photo close-out package showing the finished roof. That close-out file is what you will need if the next storm hits, because it proves the roof was new and sound before the damage, which keeps the next claim from turning into an argument about pre-existing wear.

faq.q: How can I tell if my roof has hail damage?
faq.a: From the ground, look for dents in gutters, downspouts, and roof vents, granules piled in the gutters or at the downspout outlets, and damaged window screens or AC fins. On the roof, hail leaves soft black bruises on asphalt, dents on metal, and cracks at the edges of tile. Most hits are not visible from the driveway, which is why we walk every slope rather than guess.

faq.q: What size hail damages a roof?
faq.a: Hail around one inch in diameter, roughly quarter size, is generally enough to bruise standard asphalt shingles, especially older ones. Golf-ball hail (1.75 inches) cracks tile, splits cedar, and dents most metal. Smaller hail can still strip granules from an aging roof. Shingle age, wind speed during the storm, and the slope direction all change the outcome, so the only way to know is an inspection.

faq.q: How long do I have to file a hail damage claim in Colorado?
faq.a: The deadline comes from your policy, not state law, and many policies require prompt notice or set a limit from the date of loss. Call your agent as soon as you suspect damage. Waiting makes it harder to tie the damage to a specific storm and easier for a carrier to argue wear and tear. Once a claim is approved, Colorado law gives you at least a year to complete the work and collect recoverable depreciation on most policies.

faq.q: Will insurance pay for Class 4 shingles?
faq.a: Usually only if your roof already had Class 4 shingles or your policy includes an upgrade endorsement. Otherwise the carrier pays to replace like with like, and the upgrade to Class 4 is a difference you pay out of pocket. Many homeowners choose it anyway because the premium discount offered by many Colorado insurers can recover the difference over a few years, and the roof is far more likely to survive the next storm.

faq.q: Can a roofer pay or waive my deductible in Colorado?
faq.a: No. Colorado law (C.R.S. 6-22-105) prohibits roofing contractors from paying, waiving, rebating, or advertising that they will cover any part of an insurance deductible. We never do. A contractor who offers is breaking the law, and a carrier can refuse to consider that contractor's estimate. Walk away from anyone who promises a free roof, because the money comes out of your claim or out of the quality of the work.

title: Storm Damage Roofing Colorado
description: Storm damage roofing in Northern Colorado: wind uplift, tree impact, emergency tarping, snow and ice, and claim documentation. Get a free inspection.
keywords: wind damage roof repair fort collins
lede: Hail gets the headlines, but Front Range roofs are torn up by wind, falling trees, and wet spring snow just as often. When something fails, the first job is to stop the water. The second is to document everything before it gets cleaned up.
summary: Emergency tarping and dry-in, wind uplift and tree impact repair, snow and ice damage, and claim-ready documentation for Northern Colorado and the mountains.
lifespan: Emergency dry-in holds weeks; permanent repair restores the roof's remaining service life
costRange: Emergency tarping is priced by roof area and access; permanent repair varies by damage and is often covered by insurance

sections.h2: What storm damage roofing covers
sections.html:
Storm damage work is two jobs in sequence. The first is emergency response: stop water from entering the building and make the structure safe. The second is permanent restoration, scoped and documented so your insurer pays for what the storm actually did. What we handle:

  • Emergency tarping and dry-in. Reinforced tarps battened to the roof, temporary underlayment over exposed decking, and board-up of broken skylights and vents.
  • Wind uplift repair. Lifted, creased, and missing shingles, torn ridge caps, peeled-back metal panels and membrane edges, and blown-off flashing.
  • Tree impact. Limb removal coordination, structural assessment of broken rafters and trusses, decking replacement, and full rebuild of the affected area.
  • Snow and ice damage. Ice dam intrusion, crushed gutters, collapsed overhangs, and sag on low-slope roofs that held too much wet snow.
  • Water intrusion follow-through. Photographing interior damage and coordinating with your restoration contractor so the roof scope and the interior scope match.

Hail has its own page because the inspection method is different: hail damage roof repair.

sections.h2: Front Range wind: downslope events and microbursts
sections.html:
Two very different wind events take roofs apart here. Downslope wind events hit the foothill communities from Boulder north through Loveland, Fort Collins, and Wellington from late fall through early spring. Air spills over the Continental Divide, accelerates down the east slope, and arrives as sustained winds with gusts that regularly exceed 80 mph and occasionally top 100 mph in the canyon mouths. These storms last for hours, which is what makes them destructive: a shingle seal that survives one gust fails on the two hundredth. West-facing slopes, rakes, ridges, and the corners of low-slope roofs take the worst of it.

Microbursts and straight-line winds come with summer thunderstorms, often the same storms that drop hail. A microburst is a column of air slamming down and spreading out, producing short bursts of 60 to 90 mph wind in a narrow path. The damage pattern is distinctive: one house stripped, the neighbor untouched, trees snapped in a single direction.

Wind damages a roof by uplift. Pressure differences peel at the edges and the field follows. On asphalt roofs the evidence is creased shingles that have folded back and stayed, broken seal strips you can lift by hand, and exposed nails. That is why the high-wind nailing pattern (six nails per shingle instead of four), a sealed starter course, and properly fastened drip edge matter more on the Front Range than almost anywhere else in the country.

sections.h2: Snow and ice: the slow storm
sections.html: Front Range snow damage is a spring problem. The heavy, wet storms of March and April carry far more water per inch than January powder, and a foot of it on a flat garage or a low-slope commercial roof can approach the design load, especially where it drifts against a parapet or an upper wall. On steep roofs the issue is ice dams: attic heat melts snow on the upper slopes, water runs to the cold eave and refreezes, and the ice ridge backs water up under the shingles and into the wall. Roofs built without ice and water shield at the eaves are the ones that leak. In the mountain communities, Estes Park, Winter Park, Breckenridge, and the rest, loads are higher, the season is longer, and sliding snow off a metal roof can rip gutters and crush decks below. Our post on snow load and ice dams above 8,000 feet goes deeper. Never hire anyone to chip ice off a roof with a hammer; the shingles come off with it.

sections.h2: Documenting storm damage for a claim
sections.html:
Insurers pay for what can be proven, and the proof disappears fast once the cleanup starts. Before anyone touches the roof or the yard:

  1. Photograph the roof from the ground on all sides, the debris where it landed, and the interior damage with a wide shot and close-ups.
  2. Note the date and time of the storm. National Weather Service storm reports and local news coverage establish that a wind or hail event happened at your address on that date.
  3. Keep the broken pieces. Blown-off shingles, bent flashing, and the limb that came through the deck are evidence.
  4. Call us for the dry-in. Your policy requires you to prevent further damage, and the tarping invoice is a reimbursable claim expense on most policies.
  5. Do not sign anything that assigns your insurance benefits to a contractor before the roof has been inspected and the claim has been filed.

We photograph every slope and every damaged detail, mark wind-creased shingles with chalk, and give you a written report. Once you sign with us, we meet your adjuster on site. We do not negotiate your claim; our insurance claim roofing page spells out exactly where that line is.

sections.h2: Timeline, cost, and what to expect
sections.html:
For active leaks we aim for same-day or next-day dry-in. Permanent repair timing depends on the claim: a small wind repair paid out of pocket can be done within days, while an insurance-funded replacement waits on the adjuster inspection, typically one to three weeks, and then the materials order and permit. Tree-impact jobs with structural repair add an engineer's letter and a framing inspection before the roof goes back on.

Emergency tarping is priced by the area covered and the difficulty of access; steep, icy, or three-story roofs cost more to secure safely. Permanent repair runs from a service-call minimum for a few wind-lifted shingles to a full roof replacement when the damage covers most of the roof. When insurance is involved, your cost is your deductible plus any upgrades you choose. Costs vary by roof and by storm; we put every number in writing before work starts.

sections.h2: Warranty on storm repairs
sections.html: Storm repair should carry a written workmanship warranty covering the repaired area against leaks caused by the work, for a stated term. Ask what it covers if another storm hits the same spot, because no workmanship warranty covers new weather damage. If the repair involves a partial slope replacement, confirm in writing that the new shingles are the same product line as the existing roof or an approved match, and that the manufacturer warranty on the new material is registered. For a full replacement, get the manufacturer warranty and the workmanship warranty as separate documents and keep them with your claim file and the close-out photos.

faq.q: What should I do first after storm damage to my roof?
faq.a: Stay off the roof. Move anything valuable away from active drips, put a bucket down, and photograph the interior damage. Then photograph the exterior from the ground and the debris where it fell. Call us for emergency tarping if water is coming in, and call your insurance agent to report the loss. Keep every receipt. Do not sign a contract with the first truck that pulls up.

faq.q: Does homeowners insurance cover wind damage to a roof in Colorado?
faq.a: Most Colorado homeowners policies cover sudden wind damage as a named peril, including shingles blown off and water that enters through the opening. They do not cover long-term wear, poor maintenance, or a roof that was already failing. Some policies apply a separate wind and hail deductible that is a percentage of the dwelling coverage rather than a flat amount, so read the declarations page before you file.

faq.q: How much does emergency roof tarping cost?
faq.a: It depends on how much roof has to be covered and how hard it is to reach. A single-story home with one damaged slope costs far less to secure than a steep, icy three-story roof. On most policies the cost is a reimbursable mitigation expense, because your policy requires you to prevent further damage after a loss. We invoice the tarping separately so it can go straight into your claim.

faq.q: Will insurance cover a tree falling on my roof?
faq.a: Generally yes, if the tree came down in a storm. The policy covers the roof, the structure beneath it, and usually a limited amount for removing the tree from the house. It does not usually cover removing a tree that fell in the yard without hitting anything. If a neighbor's tree hit your house, your own policy still pays first. Document the tree, the point of impact, and the interior damage before removal starts.

faq.q: How soon can you get to my house after a storm?
faq.a: For active leaks, we prioritize same-day or next-day dry-in across Loveland, Fort Collins, Greeley, and the surrounding towns, with mountain communities scheduled as road conditions allow. Full inspections after a widespread storm are usually within a few business days. Because we are based in Loveland, we are not driving in from another state, and we will still be here when you have a question about the roof next year.

name: Roof Inspections
title: Roof Inspections Northern CO
description: Roof inspections in Northern Colorado: free post-storm, pre-listing, pre-purchase, and commercial inspections with a photo report. Book yours today.
lede: An inspection that stops at the curb is a guess. We walk every slope, open the attic hatch when there is one, photograph what we find, and hand you a written report you can keep, send to your insurer, or attach to a listing.
summary: On-roof inspections for storm damage, home sales, and commercial maintenance, with a photo-documented written report and a plain recommendation.
lifespan: Annual for residential, semi-annual for commercial, and after every hail or wind event
costRange: Post-storm inspections and replacement estimates are free; pre-listing, pre-purchase, and commercial maintenance inspections are quoted by roof size and type

sections.h2: Types of roof inspections we do
sections.html:
• Post-storm inspection (free). After hail or wind, we inspect every slope, document damage with photos and test squares, and tell you whether it is worth a claim. No obligation, and you keep the report. Details on our hail damage page.
  • Pre-listing inspection. For sellers and their agents. Know what the buyer's inspector will find before they find it, fix what is cheap to fix, and put the report in the disclosure package so the roof does not become a negotiation at the closing table.
  • Pre-purchase inspection. For buyers. A general home inspector spends a few minutes on the roof, often from the ground or a ladder at the eave. We walk it, check the attic, and give you a remaining-life estimate and a repair budget you can use in the inspection objection.
  • Annual and semi-annual maintenance inspection. For commercial buildings, HOAs, and property managers. Drains cleared, seams and flashings checked, a written condition report with photos for the file, and the documentation most manufacturer warranties require. See commercial roofing.
  • Insurance condition inspection. When a carrier asks for a roof condition report at renewal or before binding a policy on an older roof.

sections.h2: What we look at
sections.html:
A roof is a system, and the surface is the least informative layer. Our inspection covers:

  • Decking. From the attic where we can get in: water stains, delamination, daylight at the eaves, and rot around penetrations. From the roof: soft spots underfoot.
  • Underlayment and ice and water shield. Checked at the eaves, rakes, and any opened detail. Older Colorado roofs often have no ice and water shield at all.
  • Flashing. Chimney step and counter flashing, headwall and sidewall, kick-out flashing, skylight curbs, and the condition of sealant.
  • Ventilation. Intake at the soffits and exhaust at the ridge or box vents, and whether they are balanced. Blocked soffit vents are the most common cause of ice dams and premature shingle aging on the Front Range.
  • Penetrations. Pipe boots, furnace and water heater flues, exhaust fans, and satellite mounts.
  • Roof covering. Granule loss, cracking, cupping, wind creasing, hail bruising, seal strip condition, and exposed nails on asphalt; dents, fastener backout, and seam condition on metal; cracked or slipped units on tile and slate; splits and cupping on cedar; seams, ponding, and membrane condition on low-slope.
  • Valleys, gutters, and drainage. Where water concentrates, and where it is getting stuck.

sections.h2: Drone versus on-roof inspection
sections.html: Drones are a useful tool and a poor substitute. We use one for steep, fragile, or unsafe roofs, which includes most slate, clay tile, and three-story homes where walking the roof risks breaking the material or the inspector. Aerial photos also give a clean overview of the pattern of storm damage across all slopes. What a drone cannot do is feel a soft deck, lift a shingle to check the seal, or see the underside of a flashing. On most asphalt, metal, and low-slope roofs, we walk it. On commercial roofs with suspected wet insulation, we add an infrared scan at dusk, which shows where saturated insulation is holding heat. For a seller or buyer, the question to ask any inspector is simple: did you walk it, and if not, why not?

sections.h2: What the written report includes
sections.html: You get a written report, usually within a business day, with: the roof type, age estimate, layers, and approximate square footage; a condition rating for each slope and each major detail; photos with captions of every finding; a remaining-life estimate with the reasoning; a prioritized list of recommended repairs with cost framing; and for storm inspections, test-square counts and collateral damage photos your insurer will recognize. The report is written for a homeowner, a buyer, a board, or an adjuster, not for us. If the roof is fine, the report says so, and that is worth something at a closing. Our guide to roof inspections before selling explains how agents use them.

sections.h2: Why Colorado roofs need a closer look
sections.html: Front Range and mountain roofs age differently from the national averages, and a checklist written for the Midwest misses it. Hail season runs May through August, and a roof that looks fine in April can have a season's worth of bruising by September. High-altitude UV strips granules and embrittles shingles faster than the warranty paperwork assumes. Ice dams leave telltale stains on the eave decking that only show from the attic. In the wildland-urban interface, from Estes Park and Glen Haven to Red Feather Lakes and Nederland, we also check for ember entry points: unscreened vents, debris in valleys and gutters, and gaps at the roof edge, because embers landing on a roof is how most homes in a wildfire are lost. For mountain homes, we look for the signs of snow load stress: sagging ridges, cracked rafters, and gutters torn loose by sliding snow. Read how long a roof lasts in Colorado for what the numbers really look like here.

sections.h2: What inspections cost and what to get in writing
sections.html:
Post-storm inspections and replacement estimates are free. Pre-listing, pre-purchase, and commercial maintenance inspections are priced by roof size, pitch, material, and access; industry pricing for a walked residential inspection generally runs from under $100 to a few hundred dollars, with drone, infrared, and multi-building commercial work priced higher. The fee is quoted before we come out and credited toward repair work when you hire us for it. Costs vary by property.

An inspection report is a condition assessment, not a warranty. If you need a roof certification for a sale or a lender, that is a separate written statement with a defined term and conditions, and it should spell out exactly what is being certified. For any inspection, get the report in writing with dated photos, the inspector's findings in plain language, and the recommendations separated from the sales pitch. If an inspector will not hand you the photos unless you sign a contract, find another inspector.

faq.q: Is the roof inspection really free?
faq.a: Post-storm inspections and replacement estimates are free with no obligation, and you keep the photo report whether or not you hire us. Pre-listing, pre-purchase, and commercial maintenance inspections carry a fee because they take longer, produce a more detailed document, and are not tied to a storm event. We quote the fee up front and credit it toward repair work if you hire us for it.

faq.q: How often should a roof be inspected in Colorado?
faq.a: Once a year for a home, ideally in the fall after hail season and before snow, plus after any storm that dented your gutters or dropped hail larger than a dime. Commercial and HOA roofs should be inspected twice a year, spring and fall, which most manufacturer warranties require. Roofs over 15 years old benefit from more frequent checks because small failures turn into deck rot faster.

faq.q: Does a home inspector check the roof?
faq.a: Usually only briefly, and often from the ground or the top of a ladder. General home inspectors are not required to walk the roof and many will not, which is why their reports often say the roof should be evaluated by a roofing contractor. A dedicated roof inspection walks every slope, checks the attic, and gives you a remaining-life estimate and repair budget you can use in your inspection objection.

faq.q: Can you certify my roof for a home sale?
faq.a: We can provide a written roof condition report with photos for a listing or purchase. If a lender or buyer asks for a roof certification, that is a separate document stating the roof is free of defects and expected to perform for a defined term, usually after required repairs are completed. We explain exactly what the certification covers and does not cover before issuing it, and we do not certify a roof we have not walked.

faq.q: What is the difference between a drone and an on-roof inspection?
faq.a: A drone gives clear aerial photos of every slope and is the safe choice for steep, fragile, or very tall roofs, including slate and clay tile that break underfoot. It cannot feel a soft deck, lift a shingle to test the seal, or look under flashing. An on-roof inspection does all of that. We walk the roof wherever it is safe to do so and use the drone where it is not, and the report says which.

name: Roof Replacement
title: Roof Replacement Loveland, CO
description: Roof replacement in Northern Colorado: full tear-off, decking, ice and water shield, ventilation, Class 4 or metal options, itemized. Get a free estimate.
lede: A replacement is the one time every layer of the roof is open and fixable. Tear it off to the deck, repair what is rotten, build the water barrier back in the right order, and ventilate it so the new roof actually lasts.
summary: Full tear-off roof replacement with decking repair, ice and water shield, balanced ventilation, and Class 4, metal, or specialty options, scoped in writing.
lifespan: 20 to 30 years for Class 4 asphalt in Colorado; 40 years and up for metal
costRange: Priced per square; typical Front Range asphalt replacements fall in a mid-four to low-five-figure range for an average home, varying by size, pitch, material, and decking

sections.h2: What a full roof replacement includes
sections.html:
A replacement done right follows the same order on every house, because water does not care about shortcuts.

  1. Tear-off to the deck. Every layer comes off. Colorado code allows two layers of asphalt, but a roof-over hides rotten decking, adds weight, and voids most manufacturer warranties. We tear off.
  2. Decking inspection and repair. Soft, delaminated, or rotten sheets are replaced, priced per sheet in the contract so there is no surprise. Older homes with plank decking may need re-sheeting to give the new fasteners something to hold.
  3. Ice and water shield. Self-adhered membrane at the eaves (at least 24 inches past the interior wall line), in every valley, and around every penetration and chimney. This is the layer that stops ice dam leaks.
  4. Synthetic underlayment over the rest of the deck. Felt tears in wind and wrinkles when wet; synthetic does neither.
  5. Drip edge at eaves and rakes, new, not reused, lapped correctly with the underlayment so water that gets under the shingles still exits over the fascia.
  6. Starter, field, and ridge. A sealed starter course at the eaves and rakes, field shingles nailed in the high-wind pattern, and ridge cap over a ridge vent.
  7. Flashing. New step flashing, counter flashing, pipe boots, and kick-out flashing. Reused flashing is the most common cause of leaks on a new roof.
  8. Ventilation. Intake at the soffits balanced with exhaust at the ridge. We calculate it rather than guess.
  9. Cleanup and close-out. Magnetic nail sweeps every day, a final property walk, and a photo package of every stage.

sections.h2: Why Colorado changes the specification
sections.html: The same shingle package that works in Kansas City is underbuilt for Loveland. Hail is the reason we treat UL 2218 Class 4 impact-resistant shingles as the default on the Front Range rather than an upgrade; many insurers discount premiums for them and Fort Collins requires them. UV at altitude ages asphalt faster, and the single biggest factor in how long shingles last here is attic temperature, which is a ventilation problem. A hot, unvented attic cooks shingles from below. Snow and ice make the ice and water shield at the eaves non-negotiable, and on mountain homes we run it further up the slope and in every valley end to end. Wind off the foothills is why every shingle gets six nails and the starter course is sealed at the rakes, not just the eaves. In the wildfire interface, a Class A fire-rated assembly and ember-resistant vents are the difference between a roof that survives an ember storm and one that does not.

sections.h2: Material options
sections.html: Most Northern Colorado replacements are architectural asphalt, and for most homes that is the right call. Within asphalt, the choice is standard architectural versus Class 4 impact-resistant, and the gap in price is smaller than most people expect once the insurance discount is counted. Beyond asphalt: metal roofing, including standing seam and stone-coated steel, for a 40-plus-year roof that sheds snow and shrugs off hail; synthetic slate and shake for the look of slate or cedar with Class 4 impact resistance and a fraction of the weight; and natural slate, clay and concrete tile, and cedar shake for homes where the architecture calls for them. Our 30-year cost comparison of metal versus asphalt lays out the real numbers. We quote the options side by side so you can see what each adds and what each returns.

sections.h2: Timeline, permits, and inspections
sections.html:
Most single-family homes are torn off and re-roofed in one to two days once materials are on site, weather permitting. We do not open more roof than we can dry in the same day. Larger, steeper, or specialty roofs take longer, and metal and tile are measured in days to a week or more. Materials typically take a few days to a couple of weeks to arrive depending on the product and the season; after a major hail storm, lead times stretch.

Roof replacement is permitted work in every Northern Colorado jurisdiction we serve. We pull the permit, schedule the inspection, and give you the approved inspection record with your close-out package. Most jurisdictions inspect at the dry-in stage (ice and water shield and underlayment down, before shingles) and at final. Some, including unincorporated Larimer County and Fort Collins, have specific requirements for Class 4 shingles and Class A fire ratings. Our Fort Collins page and the other city pages cover each local permit authority and what it looks for.

sections.h2: What a roof replacement costs in Colorado
sections.html: Replacement is priced per square (100 square feet of roof surface). On the Front Range in 2025 and 2026, installed architectural asphalt commonly runs in the range of several hundred dollars per square, with Class 4 adding a modest premium and steep, cut-up, or multi-story roofs running higher because of labor and safety requirements. Metal and specialty materials run two to three times asphalt. For a typical 25 to 35 square home, that puts an asphalt replacement in a mid-four to low-five-figure range, and metal well above it. What moves the number: roof size and pitch, number of layers to tear off, decking that needs replacing, the count of penetrations and valleys, material choice, and access. Every estimate we write is itemized so you can see each line. Read how to read a roofing estimate before comparing bids. Financing options are available if you are paying out of pocket. Costs vary by home; a free inspection gets you a real number.

sections.h2: Warranties: manufacturer, workmanship, and what to get in writing
sections.html: Two warranties cover a new roof. The manufacturer warranty covers defects in the shingles themselves. Most architectural shingles carry a limited lifetime warranty that is non-prorated for an initial period and prorated after; it does not cover hail, wind beyond the rated speed, or installation errors. Enhanced system warranties, which cover the whole assembly including underlayment and labor, are available when the full manufacturer system is installed by a credentialed contractor, and they are worth asking about. The workmanship warranty comes from the installer and covers leaks and failures caused by the installation. Get both in writing: the term, what voids them (unbalanced ventilation is a common one), whether they transfer to a buyer, and proof the manufacturer warranty was registered in your name. Ask every bidder the same questions and keep the answers with the contract.

faq.q: How long does a roof replacement take?
faq.a: Most single-family asphalt roofs are torn off and replaced in one to two days once materials are delivered. Larger or steeper homes, roofs with extensive decking repair, and metal or tile roofs take longer, from several days to over a week. We never open more roof than we can dry in before the end of the day. Material lead times add a few days to a couple of weeks, longer after a major storm.

faq.q: How much does a roof replacement cost in Colorado?
faq.a: It is priced per square and depends on roof size, pitch, layers, decking condition, penetrations, and material. A typical Front Range home in architectural asphalt lands in a mid-four to low-five-figure range; Class 4 shingles add a modest premium, and metal or specialty materials run two to three times asphalt. The only accurate number comes from measuring your roof, which we do for free and put in an itemized written estimate.

faq.q: Do I need a permit to replace my roof?
faq.a: Yes, in every Northern Colorado jurisdiction we work in. Roof replacement is permitted work with at least a final inspection, and most jurisdictions also inspect at dry-in. We pull the permit, schedule the inspections, and give you the approved record with the close-out package. A contractor who suggests skipping the permit is leaving you with an uninspected roof and a disclosure problem when you sell.

faq.q: Can you install new shingles over my existing roof?
faq.a: Code allows a second layer of asphalt over one existing layer, but we do not recommend it. A roof-over hides rotten decking, adds weight, traps heat that ages the new shingles faster, prevents proper ice and water shield installation, and voids most manufacturer warranties. It saves tear-off and disposal cost up front and costs more at the next replacement. A full tear-off is the only way to know what is under there.

faq.q: When is the best time of year to replace a roof in Colorado?
faq.a: Roofs are replaced year-round on the Front Range. Late spring through fall is ideal because asphalt shingles seal best in warm sun, but winter installs work fine with hand-sealing and dry days, and crews are more available. The worst time is the middle of hail season when storm demand stretches material lead times. If your roof is failing, the best time is before the next storm, not after it.

name: Insurance Claim Roofing

title: Roof Insurance Claims Colorado
description: Roof insurance claims in Colorado: ACV vs RCV, depreciation, supplements, code upgrades, your rights, and storm chaser red flags. Get a free inspection.
lede: A roof claim in Colorado runs on rules most homeowners never see until the storm. We document the damage, meet your adjuster once you have signed with us, and never touch your deductible. You stay in control of your claim from start to finish.
summary: Claim-ready damage documentation, adjuster meetings after you sign, scope and supplement review, and a straight explanation of ACV, RCV, depreciation, and Colorado roofing law.
lifespan: Most Colorado roof claims run 30 to 90 days from filing to completed roof
costRange: Your cost on an approved claim is your deductible plus any upgrades you choose; we never pay, waive, or rebate deductibles

sections.h2: The Colorado roof claim process, step by step
sections.html:
1. Inspection. Before you call your carrier, get the roof inspected. Filing a claim that turns out to be nothing goes on your claims history. Our free inspection tells you whether there is damage worth filing.
  2. File the claim. You call your carrier or agent, report the date of loss and the storm, and receive a claim number. Colorado regulations generally require the carrier to decide a complete claim within 60 days.
  3. Adjuster inspection. The carrier sends a field adjuster, usually within one to three weeks. Once you have signed a contract with us, we meet the adjuster on the roof and walk the test squares and photos with them.
  4. Scope and first check. The adjuster issues an estimate, called the scope, and the carrier pays the actual cash value (ACV) minus your deductible.
  5. Contract and scope review. We compare the carrier's scope line by line against the code-required work and the actual roof, and show you any gaps in writing.
  6. Supplement if needed. Missing items are submitted to the carrier with photos and code references for approval before the work starts.
  7. Build. Permit, materials, roof, inspection, close-out photos.
  8. Depreciation release. We send the final invoice and the carrier releases the recoverable depreciation, which is the balance between ACV and replacement cost.

sections.h2: What we do and what we do not do
sections.html:
Colorado draws a clear line between a roofing contractor and a public adjuster, and we stay on our side of it.

We do: inspect and document the damage with slope-by-slope photos, test squares, and measurements; give you a written report you can submit with the claim; meet your adjuster on site once you have signed a contract with us; review the carrier's scope against code and the actual roof; submit supplements for missing or code-required items with documentation; and build the roof to the approved scope with a photo close-out.

We do not: negotiate your claim or your settlement amount on your behalf; act as or claim to be a public adjuster; file the claim for you; tell you what to say to your carrier; or pay, waive, rebate, or absorb any part of your deductible. Colorado law (C.R.S. 6-22-105) prohibits that last one outright, and any contractor offering it is breaking the law and putting your claim at risk.

Your claim is a contract between you and your insurer. Our job is to make sure the information in it is accurate and complete. If you want someone to negotiate for you, that is a licensed public adjuster or an attorney, and we will tell you so.

sections.h2: ACV, RCV, and recoverable depreciation
sections.html:
Most Colorado homeowners policies pay roof claims on a replacement cost value (RCV) basis, but they pay it in two checks. The first is the actual cash value (ACV): the replacement cost minus depreciation for the roof's age and condition, minus your deductible. The second, the recoverable depreciation, is released after the work is complete and the carrier receives the final invoice. A 15-year-old roof might be depreciated 50 percent or more, so the first check can look alarmingly small; that is normal, and the balance comes when the roof is done.

Some policies, especially on older roofs or as a cost-saving option, pay ACV only, which means the depreciation is never recovered and you pay the difference. Some carry a separate wind and hail deductible of 1 to 5 percent of the dwelling coverage instead of a flat amount. Check the declarations page before you file, and ask your agent which you have. Colorado's homeowners insurance reform law gives policyholders at least 365 days to complete the work and collect the recoverable depreciation on most policies, and requires the carrier to show you its depreciation method on request. Our post on whether homeowners insurance covers roof replacement in Colorado goes further.

sections.h2: Supplements and code upgrade coverage
sections.html:
A field adjuster's scope is a first draft written in an hour on a roof. It routinely misses or undercounts items, and a supplement is the documented request to add them. Common supplement items on Front Range roofs: ice and water shield at eaves and valleys, drip edge, starter course, ridge vent, replacement of damaged decking, high-wind nailing, steep-slope and multi-story labor, and the Class 4 shingles that Fort Collins requires. Every supplement we submit includes photos, measurements, and the code or manufacturer requirement that applies.

Code-required items are paid under the policy's ordinance or law coverage, sometimes called code upgrade coverage. Most Colorado policies include some, often 10 percent of the dwelling limit, but not all, and if your policy has none the code items are your cost. This is a question for your agent before the storm, not after. If you and your carrier cannot agree on the amount of the loss, most policies include an appraisal clause under which each side hires an appraiser and the two choose an umpire; invoking it is your decision and we do not advise on it, but you should know it exists.

sections.h2: Your rights under Colorado roofing law
sections.html:
Colorado's residential roofing law, C.R.S. 6-22-101 and following, was written to deal with storm chasers. For any residential roofing contract over $1,000:

  • The contract must be in writing and include the scope of work, materials, cost, approximate dates, the contractor's contact information, and the contractor's liability insurer and surety information.
  • You may cancel within 72 hours of signing and get your deposit back. If the work is insurance-funded and your carrier denies the claim in whole or in part, you may cancel within 72 hours of that notice and receive a full refund within 10 days, less the value of any work already done properly.
  • The contractor cannot pay, waive, rebate, or promise to cover any part of your deductible, and cannot advertise that it will.
  • The contractor cannot act as a public adjuster or negotiate the claim for you, though a contractor under contract may discuss the scope of repairs with the carrier.
  • Your carrier cannot require you to use a specific contractor. You have the right to choose your own, and a carrier "preferred" program is a convenience for them, not a requirement for you.

Our storm damage page covers documenting a loss before the cleanup starts.

sections.h2: Red flags of a storm chaser
sections.html:
After every major hail storm, out-of-state crews flood Loveland, Fort Collins, and Greeley and leave when the claims dry up. The warning signs are consistent:

  • An offer to cover, waive, or "work with you on" the deductible. Illegal in Colorado.
  • A contract that assigns your insurance benefits to the contractor, or a contingency agreement signed before anyone has inspected the roof.
  • Pressure to sign today, a large cash deposit before materials are ordered, or a price that cannot be put in writing.
  • No local address you can drive to, out-of-state plates, a phone number from another area code, and no certificate of insurance on request.
  • A promise about what your insurer will pay. No contractor controls that.

A legitimate claim takes 30 to 90 days from filing to finished roof, and the work itself takes a day or two. Get the contract, the scope, the manufacturer warranty, and the workmanship warranty as separate documents, and keep the close-out photos; that file is what protects you on the next claim.

faq.q: Can a roofer waive my deductible in Colorado?
faq.a: No. Under C.R.S. 6-22-105 a roofing contractor may not pay, waive, rebate, or promise to cover any part of your insurance deductible, and may not advertise that it will. A carrier may refuse to consider the estimate of a contractor who made that offer. We never do it. If a contractor offers, the money is coming out of the quality of your roof or out of a padded claim, and both are your problem later.

faq.q: What is the difference between ACV and RCV on a roof claim?
faq.a: Replacement cost value (RCV) is what it costs to replace the roof today. Actual cash value (ACV) is RCV minus depreciation for the roof's age and condition. On a replacement cost policy the carrier pays ACV first, minus your deductible, and releases the recoverable depreciation after the work is done and invoiced. On an ACV-only policy, the depreciation is never paid and you cover the gap. Check your declarations page to see which you have.

faq.q: How long does a roof insurance claim take in Colorado?
faq.a: Most run 30 to 90 days from filing to a finished roof. The adjuster inspection usually happens within one to three weeks of filing, Colorado regulations generally require a decision on a complete claim within 60 days, and the roof itself takes a day or two once materials arrive. Supplements, disputes, and post-storm material shortages add time. Colorado law gives you at least a year to complete the work and collect depreciation on most policies.

faq.q: Do I have to use the contractor my insurance company recommends?
faq.a: No. You have the right to choose your own roofing contractor in Colorado. Carrier preferred-contractor programs are a convenience for the insurer and sometimes come with a workmanship guarantee, but they are not a requirement, and a contractor whose business depends on the carrier has a conflict you should think about. Choose a local, licensed, insured contractor with a written scope and warranties, and let the carrier adjust the claim.

faq.q: What is a roof claim supplement?
faq.a: A supplement is a documented request to add items the adjuster's original scope missed or undercounted, such as ice and water shield, drip edge, ridge vent, damaged decking, steep-slope labor, or code-required Class 4 shingles. It includes photos, measurements, and the code or manufacturer requirement that applies, and the carrier approves or denies each line. A legitimate supplement corrects the scope to match the real roof; it is not a way to inflate a claim.
